text: Here is a scene that plays out more often than anyone admits. You open the OpenAI dashboard, type $50 into the monthly spend limit, hit save, and go to bed feeling responsible. That night a background job gets stuck in a loop. By morning there is a polite alert in your inbox and the meter is still running.

Nothing broke. That is how the setting works. On OpenAI, a monthly spend limit only sends alerts unless you also turn on a separate switch called Enforce a hard limit. Most people never see the switch, because the number field looks like it is the limit.

I read the current billing docs for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google side by side on November 2, 2026. Each one does something different at the cap, returns a different error, and lets a different amount slip past. If you only remember one table from this post, make it the next one.

This is the cheapest fix in the whole post, and it takes about a minute. Go to Organization limits (or the project's limits), select Edit spend limit, enter the monthly number, turn on Enforce a hard limit, and save. Do it for the organization and again for each project that runs unattended code.

One more thing people miss: OpenAI also gives your organization its own approved monthly usage limit based on your tier. That is a separate ceiling with its own error code, organization_usage_limit_exceeded. If you see that one, your own limit is not the problem; you need to ask OpenAI for a higher approved limit.

This one is sneaky. When an Anthropic organization hits its tier cap, the API returns HTTP 429 with error type rate_limit_error. That is the exact error type you get for a normal per-minute rate limit. The difference is buried in error.details.error_code, which says enforced_spend_limit_reached, and in the missing retry-after header.

Most retry code only looks at the status code. So it sees 429, waits, retries, sees 429 again, and keeps going until it gives up. Anthropic says plainly that retrying, including the SDK's automatic retries, fails until access resumes, which can be weeks away if you hit the cap on the 9th.

Google's billing page does not spell out the error for a spending cap. Developers on Google's forum report a 429 whose message says the billing account exceeded its monthly spending cap. If you run Gemini in production, match on that message, and check it against a real response before you trust it.

The fix is the same idea everywhere: give risky work its own fence. Put experiments, evals and batch jobs in their own OpenAI project or Anthropic workspace with a small hard limit, so they hit their wall long before production hits the shared one.

On Gemini that is harder, because the tier cap lives on the billing account. A separate billing account isolates the risk but starts its own tier history from scratch, which means a low cap of its own. Decide which hurts more for you: a smaller ceiling for experiments, or the chance of an experiment pausing production.

Anthropic does not let you set a spend limit on the Default Workspace. If you never created another workspace, every key you have lives there, and the only thing standing between a bug and your card is the organization-wide limit.

Create one workspace per app or environment, move keys into them, and set each workspace's monthly limit lower than the organization's. Workspace limits cannot be higher than the organization limit anyway, so the organization number becomes your true worst case.

None of the three providers promises an instant stop. OpenAI says recorded spend can slightly exceed the limit while the limit state propagates. Google is more specific: billing data can lag around 10 minutes, and batch completions and agent sessions can run past a project cap.

Do the math for your own worst loop. Say a broken agent spends $3 a minute. Ten minutes of lag is about $30 past the cap. That is an illustration, not a measurement, but the point holds: the faster your heaviest job can spend, the lower you should set the cap below what you can actually afford.

Two Gemini details worth knowing while you are in there. Prepaid credits expire after 12 months and are not refundable, so buy what you will use. And if your Google Cloud billing account was opened after March 2, 2026, the $300 welcome credit does not pay for Gemini API usage, so it will not cushion an overrun.

Provider caps work on organizations, projects and workspaces. They know nothing about your customers. If one free-plan user scripts your chatbot, the cap will happily let them burn the whole month, and then shut everyone else out.

On October 28 and 29, 2026 we ran DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (API model deepseek-flash) and DeepSeek V4 Pro (deepseek-v4-pro) on the same 720 tasks each. Every answer was checked by plain Python code, not by another LLM. A failed answer got up to two retries, and every attempt was billed, so the cost per correct answer includes the misses.

Both models reached 100% within three attempts on both tiers. First-try success was 95% to 100% on every task for both, never more than one item apart. So on these tasks you are not buying accuracy with V4 Pro. You are buying the same answers at a higher price.

In absolute terms the whole run is cheap: $0.32 at list price for Flash's 720 items and $2.24 for V4 Pro's. The ratio is what matters once volume grows. At 100,000 everyday tasks a month, Flash comes to about $35 and V4 Pro to about $170. On hard tasks it is about $60 against $548.

The gap also grows with difficulty. On everyday tasks V4 Pro cost 4.9x as much per correct answer. On the hard tier it was 9.2x, and on the hardest single task, regex writing with leap years, Roman numerals and lookaheads, it was 14x.

If both models wrote the same number of tokens, V4 Pro would cost between 3.3x and 7.3x as much, depending on how much of the bill is output, fresh input or cached input. It cost more than that because it writes far more output, and almost all of the extra is reasoning. You never see those tokens in the reply, but they bill at the output rate.

On the hard tier V4 Pro's mean output per attempt was 1.3x to 4.3x Flash's. On hard regex items it averaged 4,294 output tokens per attempt against Flash's 1,003. A 3.3x output price times a 4.3x token count is roughly 14x, which is the gap we measured on that task.

This is the part a price table can't show you. Two models can be 3.3x apart on the rate card and 9x apart on the invoice, and the only way to find the token ratio is to run your own prompts and read the usage field on every response.

Our harness caps output at 16,000 tokens per call. Three V4 Pro attempts (two hard regex items and one bug fix) hit that cap while still reasoning and returned nothing. Each of those calls was billed for 16,000 output tokens, about $0.063 at Peak, and each item then passed on the retry. Flash never hit the cap.

Three cut-offs in 720 items sounds small, but each one costs more than 150 times what Flash spent on an average everyday answer, and produces nothing. If you run a reasoning model in production, log how often a reply ends at the token limit. Those calls don't show up as errors. They show up as a bigger bill and a retry.

Intent classification had the smallest gap, 2.3x. The answer is one short label, so there is little room for extra output. The long-document task sends a 30K-token handbook on every call, yet it cost about the same as the short tasks: about 98% of that input was served from DeepSeek's cache at $0.006 or $0.044 per million tokens. If your prompts share a long prefix, caching matters more than which of these two models you pick.

The runner works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and DeepSeek keys. It prints what a run would cost before making any call, stops before any attempt that could go past your budget, and resumes where it stopped. A full DeepSeek run like this one costs a few dollars at list price.

Our own takeaway is narrow. For work where a script can tell you whether the answer is right, start with V4.1 Flash and move a task to V4 Pro only when Flash fails it often enough to show up in your logs.

Start with the service you would actually buy. Basic text recognition is a different purchase from invoice-field extraction. The familiar $1.50 figure is a paid page rate, not a promise that every document product from that vendor costs the same. These rows use the same records and default regions as our OCR calculator, reviewed on October 30, 2026.

If your entire monthly workload is 1,000 eligible Google pages, the page charge is zero. The next paid pages use the listed tier. Crossing a volume boundary does not reprice all earlier pages. For that reason, the rest of this article compares vision models with a $1.50 paid block, not with a fictional $1.50 Google bill for the free block.

AWS region differences and conditional new-customer trials also matter. We use the default paid region and leave conditional credits out. At high volume, use the calculator's graduated monthly total. A vision model that beats $1.50 might still lose to the cheaper OCR tier. Document parsing products can return more than text, so the table is a billing comparison, not a claim of identical features.

The input charge is what the model reads. The output charge is what it writes back. Both count. Sending a page image and asking for three fields has a different cost from asking for every word on that page, even though the upload is identical. A PDF is a container; it does not have one token count that works across providers.

For Claude and Luna, assume an A4 page at 150 dpi: 1240 x 1754 pixels. Claude's estimate combines an assumed 2,250 text tokens with a 28-pixel patch image count. Luna's estimate sends the page as an image at high detail and uses 32-pixel patches with the configured multiplier. It is not a native PDF estimate with a separately extracted text layer.

The Gemini values follow Google's documented PDF path at default media resolution. Google says text pulled from a native PDF is not billed on Gemini 3 models. That only holds for the PDF path, so don't assume it for image uploads. These are cost estimates from documented rules and stated page dimensions. We have not benchmarked recognition quality or measured tokens on a sample document collection.

Here is the whole calculation. Prices are dollars per million tokens. For 1,000 pages, divide each per-page token count by 1,000 to express the total in millions. Use the same output length for every model so that the comparison answers a cost question rather than mixing four different tasks.

The first scenario returns 700 tokens per page. That is an illustrative output budget, not a conversion from pages to words. Language, punctuation, tables and JSON keys change the count. We hold input constant and change only the answer length in the second chart. Neither scenario includes a separate instruction prompt.

Haiku and Luna beat the paid OCR baseline here. Both Gemini models cost more despite their smaller inputs. Output rates explain that reversal. There is one useful exception to the output-dominates rule: Haiku's input charge still exceeds its output charge at 700 tokens. Read both sides of the formula before deciding where to cut.

Now only Haiku stays below $1.50. The extra answer length is paid on every page. Asking for a transcript and then asking for a structured copy of that transcript writes much of the information twice. If the downstream system needs only fields, request those fields directly. Shorter output is useful only if it still contains everything the task needs.

These rounded figures are an editorial snapshot for October 30, 2026. Below the line, the model costs less than the $1.50 paid block under our assumptions. Above it, it costs more. The figures are rounded to whole tokens, so don't read much into the last digit.

This is a budget boundary, not an accuracy ranking. A short reply with missing fields is not a saving. Nor does this table say Haiku can read every document well enough for your workflow. It tells you which output lengths are worth testing. Changing the input dimensions, the text-layer estimate or the OCR tier moves the boundary.

Storage, upload handling, application code and human review are outside these API totals too. Count the pages actually submitted, including pages you did not need. Dropping a blank page before the call saves its processing cost without asking any model to produce a shorter or less complete answer.

For a large archive that needs searchable text, begin with basic OCR. Page billing is easy to forecast and the higher-volume tiers can reduce the paid rate. Check the monthly free allowance before assuming a small job has any page charge. Keep the original document available so a reviewer can check a doubtful transcription.

For fields, document questions or interpretation of layout, test a vision model. Give it the schema you need and measure actual output tokens. An estimate based on 700 tokens is not useful if your accepted answers average much longer. Compare successful extraction on the same documents before making a model choice from a price chart.

A hybrid can work too: run OCR first, then send only the recognized text to an LLM. That removes the image input from the second step but adds an OCR charge. It can also lose layout clues. Try it where plain text preserves the information; keep difficult pages on a separate path that still sees the image.

Somebody on your team has done the napkin math. Open-weight models are good now, GPUs are easy to rent, and the API invoice keeps growing. Why pay per token when you could pay a flat rate and own the box?

Here is the part the napkin skips. A rented GPU starts billing the moment it boots. At $3 an hour, always on, that is $2,190 every month, and that number does not care whether the GPU answered ten requests or four million. An API is the opposite: zero requests, zero bill.

So the question is not "which is cheaper per token." It is "how many requests do I need to send before a flat $2,190 beats paying per call." Below that line, every dollar of GPU rent you pay is a dollar you handed over for idle silicon.

To make it concrete, every number in this post uses one workload: requests of 1,500 input tokens and 500 output tokens, priced at each provider's Standard list rate. On the GPU side we use the defaults from our self-hosted calculator: one GPU at $3 an hour, online 730 hours a month, sustaining 5,000 prefill and 1,500 decode tokens per second across all concurrent requests. Those GPU figures are assumptions for illustration, not benchmarks of any model.

Read that chart twice. At 100,000 requests a month, the always-on GPU costs more than running every one of those requests through Claude Opus 5.5, one of the most expensive models on the list. It costs 54.75 times what the same traffic costs on Claude Haiku 5.5. And the GPU is busy for 2.4% of the hours you pay for. The other 97.6% is rent on a machine that is waiting.

The break-even is one division: monthly GPU cost ÷ API cost of one request. Above that request count, the flat rent is cheaper. Below it, the API is. There is a second number that matters just as much: how many requests the GPU can actually serve in a month.

Two things jump out. Against frontier-priced APIs the line is low: 136,875 requests a month against Opus 5.5 is roughly 4,500 a day. If you really can replace Opus-class output with a model that fits on one GPU, that is a volume plenty of products reach.

Against the budget tier the line climbs fast, and for two models it leaves the chart entirely. To beat DeepSeek V4.1 Flash the GPU has to stay half busy every hour of every day, nights and weekends included. To beat Claude Haiku 5.5 it would need 5,475,000 requests, about 1.3 million more than it can serve. That is not a slow road to savings. There is no road.

Flip the math around and look at what one request costs you on the GPU at different volumes. The rent is fixed, so the cost per request falls as traffic grows. But it can only fall until the GPU is full.

The floor is $0.528 per 1,000 requests. Mistral Small 4 charges $0.525 for the same 1,000 requests and Claude Haiku 5.5 charges $0.40. So even a GPU running at 100%, with no spare room for a traffic spike and no engineer's time counted, loses to Mistral Small 4 by three tenths of a cent per thousand requests. A faster serving stack or a cheaper GPU can move that floor. A busier month cannot.

Nobody runs a production GPU at 100%. Traffic arrives in waves, and if the deployment is full at the peak, requests queue and latency explodes. Planning for 70% leaves room for a busy hour. That lowers the useful capacity from 4,149,473 to about 2.9 million requests a month. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash still fits under that line, but its 2,085,715-request break-even already uses about 72% of the room you planned for.

Then there is the bill that never shows up in a GPU price list: the person who keeps it running. Model updates, driver issues, a 3 a.m. out-of-memory crash. Here is what happens if you put $1,000 a month on that, say 10 hours of an engineer at $100 an hour. Pick your own number; this one is only an example.

Every break-even rises by 46%, because $1,000 is 46% of the GPU rent. On the budget side that is enough to push DeepSeek V4.1 Flash past the 70% planning ceiling. If your plan only works at 100% load with free engineering, it doesn't work.

Most napkin math assumes the GPU runs 24/7. If your traffic is an internal tool, a back-office pipeline or anything that only happens in working hours, it doesn't have to. Run it 10 hours a day on 22 workdays and you pay for 220 hours instead of 730.

That is a 70% lower break-even from changing one input. It is also the cheapest experiment you can run: if a scheduled GPU can't beat the API during the hours your traffic actually arrives, an always-on one won't either. The fine print is real, though. Every cold start pays to load model weights, on-demand GPUs are not always available the moment you ask, and anything customer-facing at night still needs a home, often the same API you were trying to leave.

One warning about the first point. Comparing a self-hosted model with Opus 5.5 only makes sense if your model passes the same test on your own tasks. A small model that needs retries or human fixes is not a cheaper Opus; it is a different product with a hidden bill. The fair comparison is against the API of similar quality for your job, which often sits in the budget tier, which brings us back to the bottom of the chart.

The example GPU above is made up on purpose. Your quote, your model and your serving stack will give different numbers, and the only throughput figure worth trusting is one you measured under realistic concurrency. Here is the quickest way to get an answer you can defend in a budget meeting:

If you run GPT-6.1 Sol in production, the launch-day pitch is hard to ignore: change one model ID and your OpenAI bill drops by half. Sometimes that is exactly what happens. Sometimes the cheaper model fails more often, you retry, a human fixes the rest, and next month's bill is higher than before. Both outcomes start with the same one-line change.

Every row has the same ratio. That makes this comparison unusually clean: for any mix of input, cached, and output tokens, a Terra request costs exactly half of the same request on Sol. Both models also have the same 1,050,000-token context window and 128,000-token output limit, so context size is not a reason to pick one over the other.

The examples below use one workload: 3,000 input tokens and 600 output tokens per request, 100,000 requests a month, Standard pricing, no caching unless a section says so. Cost per request is (3,000 × input price + 600 × output price) ÷ 1,000,000.

If Terra did your work exactly as well as Sol, the switch would save $600 a month, or $7,200 a year, on this workload. Prompt caching does not change the ratio. With 2,500 of the 3,000 input tokens served from cache, a request costs $0.003625 on Terra and $0.00725 on Sol: still half. Notice where the money goes in that cached case: output is $0.003 of Terra's $0.003625, about 83% of the request. Output length will move your bill more than input does.

Say a task is done when its answer passes your check: valid JSON, a passing test, a ticket a reviewer accepts. If you retry failed tasks until one passes, the expected cost per completed task is the cost per request divided by the success rate. Terra is cheaper when:

The gap between 45% and 90% is wide. That is good news for Terra on simple, well-specified tasks such as extraction, classification, or rewriting, where a smaller model can stay close to the larger one. It is a much tighter bet on long, multi-step work, which is where the next section matters.

The 45% rule assumes both models use the same tokens per task. The easiest way to break that assumption is to compensate for a smaller model by turning its reasoning effort all the way up. The per-token price does not change, but higher effort usually means more reasoning tokens, and reasoning tokens bill as output, the expensive side of the rate card. Agent loops do the same thing from another direction: a model that needs more steps re-sends a growing context on each one, and every step is billed.

At twice the tokens, Terra has to match Sol's success rate just to break even. Past that, no success rate makes it cheaper. So when you test Terra, try it at more than one effort setting, and try Sol one step lower than you run it today. Record the billed tokens from each response's usage field, not just whether the task passed. For agents, sum the usage across every step of the task.

Not everyone reading this runs Sol. If your traffic still sits on GPT-5.6 Terra, the math is much friendlier. GPT-5.6 Terra lists $2.00 input, $0.20 cached input, and $12.00 output per million tokens. GPT-6.1 Terra costs less on every line, and output, usually the biggest share of the bill, drops from $12.00 to $5.00.

You don't have to pick one model. If your code can tell when an answer fails, you can send every request to Terra and only pass the failures to Sol. The failed Terra call is still billed, so the route costs:

Your team switches the first model in a support workflow to one with a lower token rate. The cost dashboard confirms that an individual call is cheaper. A month later, the bill has barely moved. The agent is retrying malformed answers, sending the same retrieved context again, and asking the old model to finish the cases that the new one cannot. Each call looks inexpensive in isolation. A customer ticket still needs one accepted answer, and the path to that answer now has more calls.

That is the question a price list cannot answer: how much did the entire workload spend for each task that passed its real acceptance check? The answer might favor the cheaper model. It might favor the more reliable route. You need both the cost of every attempt and the count of accepted outcomes to tell.

Accepted tasks must be defined by the same workload acceptance rule for every route. For an API-only comparison, total workload cost includes every billed request within the stated scope, including paid failures, retries, and fallback calls. A fully loaded comparison can also include tools, infrastructure, and human review, but it must use that same boundary for every route. If no task is accepted, report cost per successful task as unavailable rather than a finite number. The worked Route A and Route B example appears below.

A token price is a useful input. It tells you what a billable unit costs under a particular provider, mode, and context tier. It does not tell you how many units a workflow will consume, how often it will retry, or whether the output will be accepted. Here is a small cross-provider snapshot from the AICostBudget canonical pricing Dataset. It is a rate-card comparison, not a ranking of model quality or task economics.

Prices are USD per million text tokens, Standard mode, at the stated base or short-context tier. Rates come from the current Dataset records, verified on the dates shown; they are not live billing data. OpenAI charges a higher tier above 272,000 input tokens for the two GPT-6 models shown; Google caching has storage charges; cache writes can have separate charges. Cached input is a rate for eligible cache hits, not a blanket discount on all input. Provider, region, mode, and token shape can change the bill. Check the date and conditions before using any row in a budget.

Luna is the lowest listed input and output rate in this four-row snapshot. That alone does not make it the cheapest model for your ticket queue, coding agent, or document pipeline. A retry resends some or all of the prompt and produces another output. A fallback may repeat the request on a different model. Failed tasks can still use billable resources. The price table supplies attempt rates; the workload supplies the attempt count and the successful-task denominator.

A successful task is a workload-specific outcome, not a model leaderboard score or an HTTP 200. For structured extraction, success might mean that required fields parse and match a checked record. For coding, tests may need to pass and a reviewer may need to accept the change. For support, the ticket may need to be resolved without reopening. Write the rule before you run the comparison, apply it to both routes, and keep tasks that fail the rule in the original incoming-task count.

Be equally precise about the boundary of a task. One customer ticket can contain several model requests. One coding assignment can contain a planner call, tool calls, a repair pass, and a final answer. If you divide spend by API requests, those pieces become unrelated rows. Give them one parent task ID, record the model and token use of each attempt, and attach the final accepted or unresolved outcome to the parent.

Use provider billing records to distinguish an unbilled provider error from a validation failure that produced a billable response. The article's worked example counts model API spend only; do not compare it with an all-in route cost unless both routes use the same expanded boundary.

Assume 10,000 incoming tasks a month. Route A uses a cheap first attempt at $0.004. Route B uses a different first attempt at $0.006. A fallback attempt costs $0.020 in either route. All attempt counts and acceptance rates below are illustrative assumptions, not benchmarked model results. The costs are examples too, not the prices of specific models in the rate card above. Your token mix and model choice would determine real attempt costs.

In this example, Route A makes 2,000 additional attempts: 1,000 on its primary and 1,000 on the fallback. It finishes with 9,000 accepted tasks. Route B makes 500 additional attempts: 400 on its primary and 100 on the same fallback. It finishes with 9,700 accepted tasks. Additional attempts here are counted across incoming tasks; they are not a claim that exactly that many distinct tasks retried.

Route A has a lower first-call price and even a slightly lower monthly API bill. Route B delivers 700 more accepted tasks for $0.40 more, so its API cost per accepted task is lower: about $0.00664 against $0.00711. The difference is not a universal savings claim. It follows only from the stated attempts, costs, and outcomes. Change any of them and the decision may reverse.

This is why reporting both cost per incoming task and cost per accepted task matters. The first tells finance what the workload spends for each job it receives. The second tells the product team what that spend buys under its acceptance rule. Neither should be silently substituted for the other.

A failed attempt can have a large input side. An agent may resend its system prompt, tools, retrieved documents, conversation history, and the error from the previous attempt. Output can grow as the agent explains and repairs its own failure. A cache hit may soften repeated input cost, but eligibility depends on the provider and on whether the prefix stays stable. Switching models or rebuilding context can lose that benefit. This is why counting retries alone is insufficient: measure tokens per attempt, including cached and uncached input.

Fallback is a distinct decision. Some systems use it for provider errors or rate limits; others escalate after a quality gate rejects a usable response. Do not call every failure a model-quality problem. If the fallback only handles a transport error and the original request was unbilled, its economics differ from a route that pays for an invalid answer and then repeats the same context. The attempt log should say why escalation happened and whether the first call was charged.

Suppose Route A's cheap first attempt still costs $0.004, but a simpler task mix allows it to accept 9,800 of 10,000 jobs without any paid retry or fallback. Its monthly API spend is $40, and its cost per accepted task is $40 / 9,800, or about $0.00408. That beats Route B's $0.00664 in the example. The cheaper model wins when its acceptance rate remains high enough, its attempts stay short, and escalations are rare. There is no rule that premium models are more economical.

A deterministic schema check can also make a smaller model practical. If it rejects malformed output cheaply, the remaining question is whether the retries it triggers buy enough accepted results. A low-cost classifier, short extraction, or routine rewrite may be an excellent fit for a low-rate model. Keep the successful workload slice separate from hard cases rather than averaging away where each route works.

If you are considering a direct move between two models, the model-switch comparison can help price the same token workload. Treat that as a first pass: it holds attempt behavior fixed. The task-level retry calculation is the next step once you know how often each route needs more work.

If you only have planning assumptions, label them as assumptions. If you have traces, replace the estimates with observed attempt counts and provider charges. Repeat the calculation after prompt, routing, model, or cache-policy changes. The useful unit is the task your user asked you to complete, and the denominator is the work your team actually accepts.

Keep the outcome ledger stable while comparing routes. If a ticket is handed to a person, decide whether the task counts as completed by the combined workflow or unresolved by the AI route, and include the person's time if you choose the former. Do not drop abandoned jobs from one candidate's denominator while counting them for the other. A weekly report can show automated acceptance beside eventual resolution, with a separate cost boundary for each. If a route needs a person to finish its hardest tickets, that work belongs in the ledger too.

The primary model is the cheapest line in your comparison. It handles one task, misses the required format, tries again, and then hands the same job to a more expensive fallback. The user sees one result. The bill records every paid attempt that led to it.

A retry is another attempt, not a correction applied for free. It may resend the system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool schemas, and user input before generating new output. An agent can add more work by planning again or repeating a tool call. A fallback can then move the extra attempt to a model with a different token price.

Keep attempt frequency separate from the final task outcome. In the calculator, T is monthly initial tasks, Cp is primary cost per attempt, r is average additional retry attempts per initial task, q is the share of those extra attempts sent to the fallback, Cf is fallback cost per attempt, and f is the final unresolved share after the workflow has finished trying.

The distinction prevents two common mistakes. First, r is not the final failure rate: 0.30 extra attempts per task does not mean 30% of tasks fail. Second, f is not a per-attempt error rate: an 8% final unresolved rate describes the tasks still unfinished after the route completes. Combining the two into one vague retry percentage hides both the extra spend and the successful-task denominator.

Assume a workflow starts 10,000 tasks per month. The primary attempt costs $0.004. The workload averages 0.30 extra attempts per initial task, so it creates 3,000 additional attempts. Forty percent of those extra attempts go to a fallback that costs $0.020 per attempt. After the retry and fallback path finishes, 8% of initial tasks remain unresolved. These are illustrative assumptions, not an industry benchmark.

The fallback handles only 1,200 attempts, but it contributes $24.00—more than three quarters of the extra-attempt cost—because each fallback attempt costs five times the primary attempt. The primary rate did not change. The route changed what one successful task costs.

The $31.20 monthly delta is retry and fallback cost under these assumptions. It is not a promised saving. Removing those attempts would also remove any successful tasks they recovered. The right comparison is not total cost with retries versus an imaginary route with perfect first-pass success. It is the current route versus a credible alternative with its own completion rate, quality, latency, and attempt pattern.

Provider price tables answer a narrow question well: what does a token cost on one model? They do not know whether your task needs one attempt or four. A request-level dashboard can also split the primary call and fallback call into separate rows, making every row look reasonable while the parent task becomes expensive.

Group attempts under a stable task ID. Then compare total cost with accepted outcomes, not HTTP responses. A 200 response can still fail a schema check. A tool call can succeed technically while moving the workflow in the wrong direction. Conversely, a second attempt can be economically justified when it turns a temporary provider error into a completed customer task.

Averages need context as well. A low mean can hide a small set of tasks that enter long loops or premium fallback routes. If those paths matter to your budget, inspect cost distributions and failure paths in production traces. The calculator intentionally estimates an average planning case; it does not claim to model p95 incidents or correlated retry storms.

A higher fallback bill can be a good trade when it materially raises completion for valuable tasks. Cutting every retry might lower the API invoice while increasing failed checkouts, unresolved support cases, or manual repair. Likewise, allowing unlimited retries can preserve a few outcomes at an unreasonable marginal cost. Neither extreme follows from the retry total alone.

Classify the reason before changing the policy. A retry after a short-lived 429 is different from retrying the same malformed prompt. A repair attempt that changes the schema instruction is different from replaying an entire agent loop. Cost data becomes actionable when it is paired with the trigger and the final outcome.

Do not optimize a rare path merely because it exists. Start when the extra-attempt share is material, the fallback tier is disproportionately expensive, or the same failure reason repeats across a high-volume workflow. A useful first pass is operational rather than theoretical.

If retries are rare and inexpensive, another cost lever may matter more. If fallback attempts dominate the delta, the primary model price may not be the first thing to optimize. The route tells you where to look; the total alone does not diagnose the cause.

The LLM Retry & Fallback Cost Calculator starts with inputs you provide: monthly initial tasks, primary and fallback models, tokens per attempt, average extra retries, fallback retry share, cached input share, and final unresolved rate. It returns base cost, retry and fallback cost, total monthly cost, successful tasks, cost per successful task, retry cost share, and the annualized delta.

It does not connect to a provider account, inspect traces, read invoices, identify your true retry rate, decide which retries are preventable, or optimize routing. Use representative assumptions when production evidence is unavailable. Once the workflow is instrumented, replace those assumptions with measured attempt and outcome data.

A fallback is one of the first reliability features you add. The cheap model handles most requests. When it fails, times out, or returns something your code rejects, a stronger model takes over. The user never sees the failure. You see it later, on the bill.

Then the obvious question shows up: the fallback fires a lot, so should you just make the stronger model the primary? Or try a different cheap model? You can answer that with two numbers: what one attempt costs on each model, and how often the fallback fires. This post works through both with current list prices, then shows how to run the same check on your own workload.

Every example below uses the same workload: 3,000 input tokens and 600 output tokens per attempt, 100,000 tasks a month, Standard pricing, no batch discount, and no prompt caching unless a section says otherwise. Prices come from the AICostBudget dataset, which links every row to the provider's own pricing page. The table at the top of this page shows each source and the date it was last checked.

Take the common setup: GPT-6 Luna as the primary, Claude Sonnet 5.5 as the fallback. A Luna attempt costs $0.0006. A Sonnet 5.5 attempt costs $0.012, which is 20 times more. When Luna's answer fails your check, you have already paid for it. Then you pay for Sonnet on top.

Now look at the bottom bar. Running Sonnet 5.5 for everything costs $1,200. The Luna route with a 50% fallback rate still costs $660. The two routes only cost the same at a 95% fallback rate. The general version of that rule is short:

If your fallback fires 30% of the time and you are tempted to go all-in on the stronger model, the math says you would pay $1,200 a month instead of $420. A high fallback rate is a signal to look at the primary model. It is almost never a reason to make the expensive model do all the work.

The more useful question is whether a different cheap primary would fail less often. A stronger primary costs more per attempt, but every fallback it avoids saves the full price of a fallback call. The switch pays off when the savings beat the extra cost:

Everything above is about quality fallbacks: the primary answered, and your code rejected the answer. Availability fallbacks are different. A 429, a 5xx, or a timeout often means the primary never produced a full answer, and the fallback is usually a model in the same price tier from another provider.

The cost people miss is the prompt cache. A cache lives with the provider that built it. Say your GPT-6.1 Sol requests reuse a long system prompt, so 2,500 of the 3,000 input tokens are cache hits at $0.10 per million. That attempt costs $0.00725. When the same request fails over to Claude Sonnet 5.5, the cache is cold, and the attempt costs $0.012. Same list price, 66% more per request.

In an LLM app, the layers are your SDK, your gateway, your own retry loop, and sometimes an agent framework on top. If each one retries, a single bad minute at the provider multiplies into a very expensive one. Pick one layer to own retries and turn the others off.

A website agent that sends leads to a CRM does a small, repeatable job. A visitor asks for a demo or a quote. The agent asks a few qualifying questions, collects an email and the details sales needs, and calls the CRM API to create or update the contact. When it works, the salesperson opens a record with the full context instead of asking the visitor everything again.

Integration guides cover the plumbing: where to ask for contact details, how to map fields, how to test the API request. They rarely cover the model bill, or what happens to that bill and to your lead flow when you swap the model behind the agent. This post works through both with current list prices.

Every number below uses one workload. One conversation is one request in the calculator. It runs six model calls. Each call resends a 2,400-token system prompt and CRM field schema plus the conversation so far, which averages 1,600 tokens. Each call writes about 150 output tokens: a reply, extracted fields, or the API request body.

The success rates are assumptions chosen to show the method, not measurements. Prices are Standard list prices from the AICostBudget dataset, with no batch discount and no caching unless a section says otherwise. The table at the top of this page links each price to the provider's own page.

Cost per conversation is (24,000 × input price + 900 × output price) ÷ 1,000,000. Input is 96% of the tokens and most of the bill: on Sonnet 5.5, input is $0.048 of the $0.057. That matters later, because input is the part caching can cut.

On tokens alone, Haiku 5.5 wins by a wide margin. It costs 5% of Sonnet 5.5 per conversation, so it only needs to succeed in 4.7% of conversations to match Sonnet's cost per successful lead at a 94% success rate. Any token-only comparison will tell you to switch today.

A lead agent is not a token-only problem. A conversation that ends without a valid CRM record is not just a wasted API call. It is a visitor who asked to talk to sales and never reached them. With the assumed rates, Sonnet 5.5 creates 18,800 complete records a month and Haiku 5.5 creates 17,600. The cheaper route loses 1,200 leads a month.

So the switch saves $1,083 a month only if each lost lead is worth less than $0.90 to you. Turn the rule around and you get the question to ask before any switch: how many points of capture rate can the cheaper model afford to lose?

To find your lead value, divide the pipeline or revenue that came from agent leads last quarter by the number of those leads. Once that number reaches a few dollars, the decision no longer turns on token price. It turns on whether the cheaper model fills the CRM fields as reliably. The mid-priced models face the same test with a smaller margin: at $50 a lead, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-5.4 mini can each afford to lose about 0.07 points.

The second move is routing. Let Haiku 5.5 handle every conversation, and send a conversation to Sonnet 5.5 only when your checks fail, for example when the extracted email is invalid or the CRM call returns an error. If 10% of conversations need that second pass and you rerun the whole conversation, the bill is $0.00285 + 10% × $0.057 = $0.00855 per conversation, or $171 a month. That keeps $969 of the $1,083 saving, as long as the second pass recovers the leads Haiku missed.

Google lists Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS at a price per million audio tokens. That number is accurate—and awkward if your budget is measured in narration minutes, podcast hours, or a localization backlog. Google's documented duration conversion makes those workloads calculable without guessing speech speed; the figures immediately below show the resulting token counts and audio-output costs.

Those are audio-output figures, not a promise about your final invoice. Gemini TTS also bills the text tokens you send. Audio dominates the round examples below, but a long script, repeated instructions, or many small generations can move the input side enough that it belongs in a real budget.

Google publishes separate text-input and audio-output rates for Flash and Flash-Lite across Standard, Batch, Flex, and Priority. Batch and Flex currently carry the same price, but they remain distinct processing modes; a shared rate does not make their API behavior interchangeable. The table keeps them on separate rows for that reason.

TTS also has two meters. The source text is input; the synthesized speech is audio output. A clean duration comparison should isolate audio first, then add measured input tokens. Blending both into a mysterious per-minute estimate makes the result look simpler while hiding the assumption that produced it.

The one-minute conversion is short: seconds multiplied by Google's documented audio-token rate. At current Standard pricing, the resulting cost is a small fraction of a dollar for either model, and Batch or Flex lowers the audio portion again. This is where four-decimal pricing matters; rounding every minute to a cent would badly distort a large forecast.

A single minute is most useful as a unit rate. It lets you multiply against measured output duration and compare modes without guessing words per minute. Speaking pace may change how much text fits into that minute, but it does not change Google's documented duration-to-audio-token conversion.

An hour converts to a much larger but still predictable audio-token count. The Standard cost gap between Flash and Flash-Lite is unlikely to decide a prototype by itself. It becomes material when the same hour is generated hundreds of times, localized into several languages, or repeated every month. The workload table keeps the exact, data-driven figures next to the durations.

The practical lesson is not that an hour is expensive. It is that the unit rate stays linear. Ten hours is ten times the output cost; one hundred hours is one hundred times the output cost. That makes a duration table reliable for budgeting as long as you keep input cost separate and do not add unsupported assumptions about retries, failed generations, or storage.

Ten thousand minutes is a useful planning unit for a large content library, a podcast archive, an audiobook pipeline, localization work, or a portfolio of voice features. It is not presented as any company's measured traffic; it is simply large enough to expose differences that disappear in a one-minute example. Its exact hours and audio-token total are shown in the computed workload table above.

At current rates, the mode decision can change the output bill as much as the model decision. The computed table shows Standard, Batch, and Flex side by side for the same duration. Whether a mode fits your system is a separate operational question; price alone does not establish eligibility or acceptable processing behavior.

For the same audio duration under current Standard pricing, Flash-Lite has a lower audio-output charge than Flash. The computed comparison below reports both the absolute difference and the percentage reduction for 10,000 minutes. The percentage holds for other durations because both models use the same documented conversion and the calculation is linear.

That statement is intentionally narrow. It says what the verified rate cards do to an equal audio workload. It does not say Flash-Lite sounds worse, Flash sounds better, or either model is the right production choice. Voice suitability needs listening tests with your scripts, languages, style controls, and acceptance criteria.

Current Batch and Flex audio rates are half their Standard counterparts for both models. The math is immediate: the same 15 million output tokens cost half as much. Priority moves in the other direction, with a higher rate than Standard. A useful cost review should therefore ask which processing mode the workload actually uses before debating small prompt optimizations.

Do not read the matching Batch and Flex prices as matching products. Google documents them as separate modes and exposes each independently. Confirm availability and processing semantics in the official documentation, then run the exact mode through the calculator. The article shows the economic range; it does not choose an operating model for you.

Google's current Gemini 3.8 TTS rates end on December 31, 2026, and the published future period starts January 1, 2027. The data-driven table below shows both Standard audio-output rates and their workload effect; text-input rates change in the same period. A forecast that crosses New Year's Day should not extend the launch-period numbers indefinitely.

For a recurring 10,000-minute monthly workload, the table reports the added monthly audio-output spend and its twelve-month impact for each model. This is a clean price-period comparison: it assumes the same duration every month and excludes text input, retries, and other services.

Duration answers the biggest question, but it is not the whole request. Suppose one Standard Flash generation produces 60 minutes of audio and sends 12,000 text input tokens. The audio side remains 90,000 tokens. The input side is priced independently at the model's current text-input rate, then added to the output charge.

The example is deliberately simple. It does not claim that every hour of speech contains 12,000 input tokens, because tokenization, markup, instructions, and language differ. Use the token count from a representative API request. For a monthly plan, multiply each generation's full cost by the number of generations rather than multiplying audio alone.

Provider pricing can change, and an invoice can include usage that a duration-only example cannot see. Treat these calculations as an auditable planning layer: the conversion is explicit, the pricing period is explicit, and the text-input caveat is visible. Then compare the estimate with your billing export once real traffic exists.

If you are thinking about moving a production workload from GPT to Claude or Gemini, the price-per-million table is where the decision starts—not where it ends. Your bill is shaped by how much context goes in, how much text comes out, how often the call runs, and how many attempts it takes to get an acceptable result.

That distinction is easy to miss. A candidate model can advertise a lower input rate while leaving the expensive output side nearly untouched. It can also generate longer answers, miss a reusable cache prefix, or need a retry on cases your current model handles once. The cheaper token can become the more expensive completed task.

Most comparison pages normalize prices to one million tokens. That makes rate cards readable, but it removes the shape of the workload. A document pipeline that sends 20,000 tokens and returns 500 is not economically similar to a report generator that sends 2,000 and returns 4,000. Multiplying both by a single blended price hides the part of the request that is actually expensive.

Monthly volume matters just as much. Saving a fraction of a cent on one call sounds trivial. Across 500,000 support conversations, it can fund a serious evaluation. The reverse is also true: a projected $40 monthly saving rarely justifies a week of prompt tuning, regression testing, and integration work.

The first pass should hold these workload quantities constant. That isolates the rate-card difference. The second pass should replace the equal-token assumption with measured candidate behavior: its tokenizer, output length, retry rate, tool loops, and task success. Mixing those two passes makes it hard to tell whether a saving came from price or from changed behavior.

These are planning scenarios, not benchmarks or claims about model quality. They use Standard, global, non-cached text rates and hold token counts constant on both sides. The figures are generated with the same calculation function and verified pricing data as the Model Switch Cost Calculator, so the examples do not maintain a parallel set of price constants. The strict catalog exposes only models whose current records satisfy its evidence and billing-semantic rules; eligible Google models can now be selectable, while the three fixed scenarios below remain GPT and Claude comparisons.

The input-heavy example rewards the lower GPT-5.4 mini input rate, but the saving is smaller than a simple input-price comparison suggests because Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4 mini are closer on output. The output-heavy example shows how sharply a smaller-model switch can move a generation-heavy bill: GPT-5.4 mini's lower output rate does most of the work because four out of every six workload tokens are generated output.

The mixed support example is deliberately a cost increase. Switching is not synonymous with saving. If the target costs more under the equal-token assumption, it needs to earn that premium through better task success, fewer retries, shorter completions, lower operational risk, or some other measured benefit. A calculator should be willing to tell you not to move.

Repeated system prompts, tool definitions, repository context, and long conversation prefixes can make cached input the main economic variable. But cache arithmetic is not just uncached input multiplied by a discount. Some providers charge for cache writes, cache lifetimes differ, prefixes must remain eligible, and a router that changes models mid-session can throw away a useful cache entry.

Do not add a guessed 70% hit rate to make a proposal look complete. Pull cache-read and cache-write usage from provider responses, group it by feature, and model misses separately. The switch calculator accepts a user-entered cached-input share only when both selected tiers have reliable verified read prices; it does not detect your hit rate. Cache-write tokens are a separate input, priced only when the tier lists exactly one verified cache-write price.

API invoices count tokens. Your product pays for outcomes. If a cheaper model succeeds on 80% of tasks and the current model succeeds on 95%, the raw per-request saving has to absorb retries, fallbacks, support work, and failed user journeys. For agent workflows, one bad tool decision can add several more calls and resend a large context each time.

This is where a representative eval set earns its keep. Run both models on real inputs, score the output with the acceptance criteria your product already uses, and record billed tokens for every attempt. Public benchmarks can help form a shortlist. They cannot price your extraction schema, support policy, tool chain, or tolerance for wrong answers.

Compare those one-time and ongoing costs with the annualized API difference, not one month of savings. A migration that saves $150 per month and consumes several engineer-days has a very different payback period from one that saves $30,000 per year.

The first useful answer is whether the rate-card difference is large enough to justify an evaluation. If it is negligible, keep the current route unless another operational requirement matters. If it is material, the projected annual difference becomes your evaluation budget—and your warning not to skip the quality work.

Switch when the cost per accepted task improves and the annual saving clears the migration cost with room for uncertainty. Stay put when the only winning number is the one printed beside a million tokens.

Yesterday's model-cost spreadsheet may already be stale. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol and Luna below their GPT-5.6 predecessors' promotional rates. Anthropic answered the same day with Claude Opus 5.5, lower list prices, and a claim that typical workloads cost about 40% less than on Opus 5. The price floor moved again—and the headlines don't show what output, caching, long context, and faster processing will do to your bill.

Anthropic's roughly 40% lower-cost statement describes typical workloads. Its launch post attributes that result to lower token prices plus lower token use, and reports 40–50% lower cost on its agentic coding tasks. It does not say every token category is 40% cheaper. Both facts can be true: the rate card can fall 20% while a model that finishes a task with fewer turns and output tokens cuts the workload bill further.

The examples below use Standard, global, short-context API rates. Every OpenAI request is assumed to stay at or below 272K input tokens. They exclude regional uplifts, Batch, Flex, Fast, provider tools, retries, negotiated discounts, and taxes. Each old/new pair holds token volume constant to isolate the published rate change; it does not assume equal model quality or equal tokens per successful task.

*The cache-heavy case uses 10M fresh input tokens, 10M five-minute cache-write tokens, 80M cache-read tokens, and 20M output tokens. It assumes every written prefix is reused as stated. A miss moves tokens back to the uncached category; a rewritten prefix can create another paid write. Opus uses the five-minute write rate in both generations so the comparison does not mix cache lifetimes.

A RAG system, coding agent, or support assistant may resend a large stable prefix: system instructions, tool schemas, repository context, or a knowledge bundle. On GPT-6, an eligible write costs 1.25 times fresh input and a later read costs one tenth. One write plus one full read therefore costs 1.35 times ordinary input, versus twice the input cost for processing the same prefix uncached twice. The saving grows only if the prefix remains stable and requests actually reach a reusable entry.

The new rates justify a migration test, not an automatic migration. Price per token is not cost per successful task. A cheaper successor can lose through extra reasoning, tool turns, cache misses, retries, or fallbacks. A pricier model can win with fewer attempts. The rate card starts the comparison; your traces finish it.

September 22 was not a same-model discount event. It brought successor launches with new price records. Preserving that distinction keeps dashboards from rewriting the historical cost of GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Luna, or Claude Opus 5.

Anthropic says Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 will follow in the coming weeks. They are not treated here as released, API-live, or priced models. When those facts change, use published records rather than extrapolating from Opus 5.5.

For 1,000 pages in AWS US West (Oregon), outside the free tier, Amazon Textract DetectDocumentText lists $0.0015 per page: $1.50 for text recognition. AnalyzeExpense lists $0.01 per page in the same region and volume band: $10 for invoice or receipt data extraction. These are two different APIs for two different jobs, not a hidden surcharge on one OCR request. If your application needs a vendor name, total, dates, or line items in structured fields, the $1.50 text-only quote does not describe that task. If plain searchable text is enough, the $10 expense API may be unnecessary.

Page price is only the first layer. Real invoice-processing cost also depends on document length, extra processing attempts, human review, downstream work, and how many submitted documents your business accepts. Use the planning calculator below with your own assumptions; it does not predict extraction quality.

An OCR API may return words and their positions. A layout or document parsing API may preserve reading order, tables, and key-value relationships. A specialized invoice processor may return normalized fields such as supplier, invoice date, amount, tax, and line items. Those outputs overlap, but they are not interchangeable. The cheapest way to obtain text is not necessarily the cheapest way to produce a usable accounts-payable record.

AWS's published US West (Oregon) examples put DetectDocumentText at $0.0015 per page and AnalyzeExpense at $0.01 per page for volumes below one million pages per month. At 1,000 pages, that is $1.50 versus $10. Both rates are list-price examples outside the free tier. The comparison isolates the API choice; it does not say that every invoice pipeline must run both APIs or that every customer will pay those amounts.

Each row assumes all pages are processed by just the named API in Oregon, all are in the first million-page tier, and no free allowance applies. For example, 10,000 × $0.0015 = $15 for text, while 10,000 × $0.01 = $100 for AnalyzeExpense. These are alternative API-only scenarios, not a prediction of your total bill. AWS documents lower rates after one million pages; the simple multiplication above should not be extended beyond that tier.

New AWS customers may qualify for a three-month free tier. AWS lists up to 1,000 DetectDocumentText pages per month, but only up to 100 AnalyzeExpense pages per month during that eligible period. Eligibility and timing matter: neither allowance should be silently applied to an established paid account. If you use the website calculator for AWS text OCR, turn on its trial option only when your account qualifies. The calculator does not expose AnalyzeExpense and cannot apply its separate allowance to an invoice estimate.

Google's Enterprise Document OCR price card lists the first 1,000 OCR pages at $0 and then $1.50 per 1,000 pages through its next published tier under the standard consumption model. That allowance applies to that OCR processor; it is not a blanket free allowance for specialized parsers. The Invoice Parser is listed at $0.10 per count under the standard consumption model, and Google defines one count as up to 10 pages in a document.

That distinction changes the math. One thousand separate, single-page invoices represent 1,000 Invoice Parser counts, or $100 at $0.10 per count under those assumptions. One hundred invoices of 10 pages each represent 100 counts, or $10. Both groups contain 1,000 pages, but they do not produce the same specialized-parser estimate. These are arithmetic illustrations, not claims that both document sets have the same business value, support conditions, or quality. Check request limits, supported document types, and your contracted consumption model before use.

The calculator compares five named products, not five interchangeable invoice processors. Alongside Amazon Textract DetectDocumentText and Google Enterprise Document OCR, it displays Azure Document Intelligence Read, Cohere Parse v5, and Mistral OCR 4.1. Azure Read is a text-reading product, while Cohere Parse and Mistral OCR produce richer document parsing output. Neither a capability label nor a low page price proves that an API returns the exact invoice fields your accounting system expects.

Cohere advertises Parse v5 at $1.50 per 1,000 pages through its API, and Mistral lists OCR 4.1 standard processing at $4 per 1,000 pages. Those are useful rate-card facts, not evidence that either product is a drop-in replacement for AnalyzeExpense or Invoice Parser. Azure's public pricing page describes separate Read and prebuilt invoice meters but may render the regional price as a placeholder; inspect the tool's cited price record and verify your own Azure region and SKU before relying on a number.

Start with a representative document set. Count pages and documents separately, record document type and region, and write down the fields the application must return. Then choose the smallest API output that meets the acceptance criteria. If text OCR is followed by a parser or language model, price that second call explicitly. If one specialized API already includes OCR in its output, do not assume a separate OCR call is required. Finally, estimate retries, storage, and human review as separate, measured or labeled assumptions.

The formula is a checklist, not an estimate with invented values. A production integration may also face limits, unsupported files, compliance requirements, and exception handling. Test your real documents and keep failed or reviewed items in the denominator when you calculate cost per accepted invoice. A cheap page price cannot compensate for an output that requires expensive repair, but that repair cost must be measured rather than guessed.

AICostBudget accepts a monthly page count and estimates the five products named above using its currently verified pricing records. It displays the applied pricing tiers, applicable unconditional allowances, an optional AWS new-customer trial, AWS commercial region choices, verification dates, and links to official sources. You do not upload a sensitive document for this estimate; the calculation runs in your browser. A stale or incomplete price is excluded from its cheapest-price ranking.

Its ranking is a cost-only result for the products and assumptions shown. It cannot decide which API will meet an invoice-field schema, compare extraction accuracy, estimate AnalyzeExpense or Google's Invoice Parser, infer document counts from pages, or calculate a complete invoice automation bill. Use it to narrow a page-priced OCR budget, then create a separate worksheet for specialized extraction and operational steps.

If the job truly ends at searchable text, a text OCR estimate may be the right starting point. If it ends at a posted invoice record, treat field extraction and validation as part of the definition of the job. The useful comparison is between implementations that deliver the same accepted output, with each billable step shown plainly.

The broad search result is already crowded with benchmark tables, launch summaries, and the same observation: the models share headline standard prices but differ on cached input and long-context economics. Repeating those tables would create little information gain and would overlap AICostBudget's existing model-comparison coverage. The unanswered buyer question is narrower: at what measured success rate does one model overcome the other's attempt cost for a specific agent workflow?

That question has a falsifiable answer. It does not require an invented universal token multiplier or a cherry-picked benchmark. It requires one representative task set, one harness, a complete cost trace, and an acceptance rubric. This article therefore treats the price card as an input to a break-even test rather than as the verdict.

The live table above is the pricing source for this page. It reads the site's verified canonical records rather than duplicating a second set of article constants. At the current standard tier, both models list the same new-input and output rates. Claude Fable 5.1 lists a lower cached-input read rate. GPT-6 Astra applies higher input, cache, and output rates to the full request when prompt input exceeds 272,000 tokens.

Do not silently treat cache writes as reads. OpenAI documents separate uncached input, cached input, and cache-write token categories for supported models. Anthropic separately prices five-minute writes, one-hour writes, and cache hits. A calculator that applies the read discount to every prompt token will understate the bill.

Total task cost means the entire chain under one parent task ID: initial request, later tool-loop calls, prompt cache writes and reads, reasoning and visible output, failed attempts, fallbacks, provider-priced tools, and any model call used to judge or repair the result. Accepted tasks means outputs that pass the same pre-declared tests or review rubric. Do not use requests completed, HTTP 200 responses, or cache hits as the denominator.

Multiply Fable's measured success rate by the worksheet's Astra-to-Fable attempt-cost ratio. That is the Astra success rate needed to tie on API cost for the fixed token shape. Because success cannot exceed 100%, divide 100% by that ratio to find the highest Fable success rate at which reliability improvement alone could still make Astra break even. The worksheet reports this feasibility ceiling explicitly. Above it, Astra must also consume fewer tokens, avoid retries or tool loops, stay below its long-context pricing threshold, or deliver another measurable benefit.

This is why a universal winner would be false precision. The ratio changes when your cache share, output length, prompt size, effort level, retry policy, and acceptance rate change. A break-even equation makes the uncertainty inspectable instead of hiding it inside a recommendation.

Aggregate the fields twice: once by provider request for invoice reconciliation, and once by parent task for unit economics. The second view is what tells you whether a cheap first attempt merely moved cost into a fallback. It also exposes workflows where a small number of pathological tasks consume most of the budget.

The cached-input rate is not the same as the effective cache saving. Effective saving depends on how much of the prompt is actually eligible, how often the stable prefix is reused, how many writes are required, and whether the next call arrives before expiration. Prompt order matters: frequently changing content placed before stable instructions can shorten the reusable prefix.

OpenAI's current prompt-caching documentation describes a 30-minute default TTL for supported GPT-5.6-and-later cache writes and reports cached, cache-write, and total input token details. Anthropic documents a five-minute default write and an optional one-hour write at a higher rate. Those are product rules, not a reason to assume your application achieves a particular hit percentage.

Community reports show why the distinction matters. A recent Reddit post described a 97.5% cache-hit rate that still obscured major output-cost changes, and commenters recalculated the claimed unit economics using the delivered-item denominator. A GitHub issue from a tool-heavy agent project reported uncached tool schemas dominating repeated input. These are useful failure modes to test, not representative market averages.

GPT-6 Astra's context window is large, but the billing step arrives much earlier than the maximum window. OpenAI states that a prompt above 272,000 input tokens receives twice the input and cache rates and 1.5 times the output rate for the entire request. This is not a marginal surcharge applied only to tokens beyond the boundary.

The worksheet makes that discontinuity visible by comparing one 200K prompt with one 300K prompt under an otherwise controlled shape. Both examples are illustrative. They do not predict the tokenization of your repository, the amount of context either model needs, or the probability that a longer prompt improves the answer.

For both models, reasoning can create billed output that is not identical to the text shown to the user. OpenAI's response limit includes visible output and reasoning tokens. Anthropic states that thinking tokens are billed as output and that prior thinking blocks retained in context can be billed as input. A comparison based only on visible answer length will therefore miss part of the bill.

Tool loops add another multiplier. Each call can produce output arguments, return new uncached context, and trigger more reasoning. Fix a maximum loop count and classify early exits. If one model finishes in fewer turns, that token-efficiency advantage belongs in the workload trace. If it stops early but fails acceptance, it does not.

The word starts is deliberate. A rate-card advantage is not a production verdict. The model with the lower attempt price can lose if it consumes more tokens or succeeds less often. The model with the higher attempt price can lose even with a small quality lead if the task has a cheap deterministic validator and easy retry.

Do not optimize the router against the same evaluation set indefinitely. Hold back a fresh validation set and watch production drift. Model behavior, prices, SDK fields, and cache rules can change. Store the model ID, pricing verification date, and policy version with each result so a future comparison remains auditable.

The worksheet is an illustrative pricing calculation, not observed production traffic and not a benchmark. Equal token shapes are intentionally artificial. The page does not claim an average success rate, retry rate, cache-hit rate, reasoning-token count, or human repair cost for either model. Those values require your application data.

Price facts come from current official provider documentation and the site's verified canonical pricing records. Community posts and issue reports are cited only as examples of operational pain. They are self-reported, may use different harnesses or incentives, and should not be generalized. Your provider invoice is the final billing source.

The clean comparison begins with like-for-like standard API billing. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Fable 5.1 both charge separately for new input, cached input, and generated output, but their product positions are different. Gemini is a Flash model designed for fast, scalable agentic work. Fable is Anthropic's premium model for demanding reasoning and long-running projects. A price table can normalize the billing units; it cannot normalize the amount of work each model performs or the quality of the finished result.

Input and output prices currently produce the headline contrast. Cache reads produce a much smaller gap because Anthropic discounted that component aggressively. This matters for coding agents, research systems, document workflows, and enterprise assistants that repeatedly resend a stable system prompt, repository map, policy corpus, or tool instructions. If your workload is mostly fresh input and long output, base rates dominate. If most of the prompt is a valid cache hit, the cache-read row becomes more important.

A token price answers one narrow question: what does the provider charge for a unit of eligible input, cached input, or output? An agent budget asks several additional questions. How many planning turns occur? How much hidden reasoning is billed? How often does the model call search, code execution, a browser, or another tool? Does a failed tool call create a retry? Does a weak first attempt trigger a premium fallback? Does the result pass tests, satisfy a reviewer, and avoid later repair? None of those variables is contained in the list price.

The denominator is the strategic part. A cheaper attempt that succeeds can be extraordinarily economical. A cheaper attempt that repeatedly fails can waste tokens and engineering time. Conversely, a premium attempt is not automatically efficient merely because it is more capable. If both models solve the job at the same acceptance rate, the lower-priced route wins. If Fable's completion rate is higher, the question becomes whether that quality advantage is large enough to offset the measured cost difference for this exact workflow.

Avoid converting vendor positioning into assumed success rates. Coding benchmarks, model cards, and customer examples help select candidates, but they do not predict your repository, tool permissions, prompt design, latency limit, or definition of done. The defensible decision is an evaluation: replay representative tasks, freeze the harness, log every billed token and tool turn, and have the same acceptance rules score both outputs.

Fable 5.1 keeps Fable 5's base input and output prices while making cache reads one quarter of the earlier model's rate. Anthropic says this reduces typical token-billed workloads by about 25 percent and can reduce complex coding and highly agentic workloads by up to about 45 percent. Those are Anthropic's measured workload claims, not a guarantee for every application. The benefit depends on how much of the input is reused successfully and how much spend comes from output or uncached tokens.

The important distinction is cache read versus cache write. Reusing an eligible prompt prefix is cheap; creating or refreshing the cache has a separate price. A long agent session with stable instructions and repository context can accumulate many reads after the initial write. A workflow that starts a fresh context for every subtask, mutates the beginning of the prompt, or waits beyond the selected cache lifetime may capture less of the discount. Measure cache-write and cache-read tokens separately rather than applying one blended discount to all input.

Google says Gemini 3.8 Flash can deliberately use more tokens on long-running and complex tasks. The model may take smaller reasoning steps, call tools iteratively, and verify its work. That behavior can be desirable: an agent that checks its own changes may avoid a failed deployment or a human review cycle. It also means the apparent price advantage should not be multiplied by a fixed token estimate copied from a different model.

Tool calls can expand both sides of the ledger. The model generates arguments, receives tool output as new context, reasons about the result, and may call another tool. A coding agent can read files, search symbols, edit code, run tests, inspect failures, and repeat. A research agent can search, open sources, reconcile conflicts, and draft. A low per-token price makes those loops affordable, but an unconstrained loop still has no meaningful budget ceiling.

Gemini exposes low, medium, and high thinking levels, with medium as the documented default. Use high effort only where the additional reasoning improves acceptance enough to justify the tokens and latency. Routine classification, extraction, drafting, and deterministic transformations may need less. The model choice and the effort setting are separate routing decisions, and both belong in the cost log.

The calculated workload above intentionally gives both models the same token shape. That isolates price and provides a reproducible baseline, but real agents rarely consume identical tokens. The next step is not to invent a token multiplier for either model. It is to measure the traces. Record new input, cached input, output including billed reasoning, tool-call count, retries, elapsed time, and accepted completion for every task.

Then calculate two views. First, cost per attempted task reveals operational spend and capacity. Second, cost per successful task connects spend to value. Add a third business measure when appropriate: cost per merged change, resolved ticket, approved report, or completed customer workflow. The closer the denominator is to the outcome your product sells, the more useful the model decision becomes.

Benchmarks are useful for screening, not for declaring a universal winner. Google positions Gemini 3.8 Flash for long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents, and complex enterprise workflows. Anthropic positions Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning, long-running agentic coding, multistep research, and difficult document work. Both vendors publish strong results, but they do not report every model on the same harness, settings, safeguards, task version, or cost accounting method.

Artificial Analysis offers a cross-provider comparison across intelligence, speed, price, context, and cost per task. That independent view is more comparable than placing two unrelated vendor charts side by side, but it still represents a benchmark suite rather than your production workflow. Check the selected reasoning effort, fallback policy, date, and methodology before importing any number into a business case.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is the stronger economic default when tasks are high-volume, the quality threshold is reachable, and the workflow benefits from fast iteration or broad multimodal input. Examples include routine code transformations, repository triage, test generation, data extraction, document classification, multimodal review, and first-pass research. Its lower current input and output prices create substantial headroom for experimentation and parallel attempts.

It is also attractive when your architecture already has deterministic validation. A compiler, unit test suite, schema validator, policy engine, or human approval step can catch failures cheaply. In that setting, the model does not need to be trusted blindly; it needs to produce enough accepted results at low total cost. Use lower reasoning effort for predictable work and raise it only when measured acceptance improves.

Fable 5.1 can justify its premium when the task is difficult, long-running, context-heavy, and expensive to repair. Anthropic specifically positions it for ambitious coding projects, complex code review, multistep research, and work that spans applications or takes hours. If your own evaluation shows fewer failed loops, higher acceptance, less supervision, or materially lower repair time, the premium can be rational even when the token bill is higher.
