The cache-read cut is most relevant when a large stable prefix is reused many times. A mature coding harness may repeatedly load repository instructions, architecture notes, tool definitions, and a substantial code map. A research or document agent may reuse a corpus and policy layer over many turns. In those cases, cache-read share can dominate input economics, narrowing the practical difference from the base-price headline.

A single winner is attractive for a headline and often wrong for a production system. Model routing lets each price and capability profile serve the work it handles efficiently. Gemini can take routine, high-volume, latency-sensitive steps. Fable can receive tasks that are classified as difficult, fail a deterministic check, exceed a complexity threshold, or carry enough value to justify premium reasoning.

The route should be observable and bounded. Give every business task a parent ID. Attach all model attempts, tool calls, cache usage, retries, and fallbacks. Record why escalation occurred and whether the final result was accepted. Without that trace, a routing architecture can look cheap in one provider dashboard while hiding duplicate spend in another.

Gemini 3.8 Flash launched on September 2, 2026 with introductory standard pricing of $0.75 per million input tokens, $3.75 per million output tokens, and $0.075 per million cached-input tokens. Google states that this introductory period ends after December 31, 2026. Standard pricing becomes $1.50 input, $7.50 output, and $0.15 cached input on January 1, 2027. Those figures are a dated launch snapshot, not a permanent current-price constant.

A forecast that covers 2027 must not multiply September rates across the whole year. Split the budget at the effective date or use the active canonical record for each period. The headline input/output gap versus Fable narrows materially when Gemini's standard rates double, although Gemini remains cheaper on those list-price components under the published rates. Re-run every monthly workload, margin model, and routing threshold before the change.

Start with 30 to 100 representative tasks rather than one impressive demo. Include easy, ordinary, and difficult cases in proportions that match production. Freeze the prompt, tool permissions, repository state, timeout, and acceptance rules. Run each model at a documented effort setting. If a model requires different prompting, allow a separate tuned prompt, but record the tuning work and do not compare a polished configuration with an untuned default.

Finally, test sensitivity. What happens if cache hits fall by half? What if Gemini uses twice the tokens? What if Fable improves acceptance by five measured percentage points? What if the Gemini rate changes in January? A robust route should remain economical across plausible ranges rather than depending on one fragile assumption.

Choose Gemini 3.8 Flash as the first model to evaluate when cost, speed, scale, multimodal input, or high-volume agent steps dominate. Its current list-price advantage is too large to ignore. Choose Claude Fable 5.1 when the task is genuinely demanding and your own results show that its long-horizon behavior, cache economics, or higher acceptance rate saves enough retries and repair to justify the premium.

Do not buy either model from a benchmark headline or a per-token ratio. Price the complete trace, divide by successful outcomes, and route accordingly. The durable conclusion is not that one provider wins. It is that list price is only the numerator of an attempted call, while cost per successful task is the economic measure that connects model behavior to product value.

RAG chatbot cost is different from ordinary chatbot cost because retrieval adds a second input stream. A user may ask a short question, but your system may retrieve several document chunks and place them inside the prompt so the model can answer from company knowledge.

This is why retrieval augmented generation cost should be modeled per resolved answer, not only per user message. A short support question can become a large API call when it carries several long help center chunks.

A SaaS help center RAG bot handles more varied questions: billing, setup, integrations, troubleshooting, security, refunds, and account workflows. The retrieved context is usually larger because the answer must be grounded in product documentation.

An internal team AI assistant can look smaller than a public SaaS chatbot because the employee count is limited. But cost can rise quickly when every employee asks many questions and each answer retrieves long documents, runbooks, policies, or customer notes.

Retrieved context tokens are the reason an AI knowledge base chatbot cost estimate can surprise teams. The user sees one question and one answer, but the model may receive the question plus several chunks of help docs, product pages, ticket history, policy text, and formatting instructions.

RAG cost reduction should keep answer quality intact. The goal is to send less irrelevant context, generate the right amount of output, and route each question to the least expensive model that still produces a trustworthy answer.

Cheaper models can work well for simple retrieval answers, classification, routing, citation formatting, and short summaries. They are risky when the retrieved context is ambiguous, the question affects billing or policy, or the answer must reason across several documents.

To model your own vector database chatbot cost and LLM API cost, start with three scenarios: low usage, expected usage, and high usage. Keep retrieved context tokens separate from user question tokens so the estimate shows the real RAG cost driver.

These are Standard short-context rates. A 12-hour cache write costs more than a normal input token, so it saves money only when the same prefix is read from cache enough times within 12 hours to recover the write premium.

The September releases change the available model ladder and the price of cached input on the newer Sol route. They do not prove that every existing workload should migrate or that every dollar saved on tokens survives changes in output length, retries, and task success.

After any OpenAI API pricing update, rebuild the estimate from the request shape. Keep input and output tokens separate because they can be priced differently and they respond to different product decisions.

Split fresh and cached input before applying the formula. For GPT-6.1 Sol, an eligible cached read is priced at 5% of ordinary input; GPT-6 Sol and Luna use 10%. Cache writes are billed separately at 1.25 times ordinary input. Do not apply the read discount to every repeated-looking token.

These light, medium, and heavy planning scenarios use the site's verified pricing dataset and the same tier-aware cost calculation as the calculators. Each holds input tokens, output tokens, and request volume constant to isolate the published rate-card difference. They are not benchmarks and do not assume equal capability.

Batch API pricing matters when your workload does not need an immediate response. Examples include nightly enrichment, evaluations, report generation, support-ticket labeling, embedding refreshes, and large CSV-style processing. If OpenAI offers a Batch API discount for the model and endpoint you use, the same job may cost less than a synchronous request route.

The September timeline is now concrete: GPT-6 Sol and Luna launched on September 22, and GPT-6.1 Sol followed on September 29 with the same short-context input and output rates as Sol but a lower cached-input rate. These are serious routing candidates, not automatic replacements.

Price the current and target routes with the same workload first. Then rerun the comparison with measured candidate output length, cache hits, retries, and task success. The decision is finished only when cost per accepted task improves—not when one row in a token table is lower.

The phrase openai api cost for 10000 users sounds simple, but it hides the important variables. A SaaS product might have 10,000 registered users, 2,000 daily active users, and 20,000 AI calls per day. Another product with the same user count might have 500 daily active users and 1,500 AI calls per day.

Use this formula for an OpenAI API monthly cost calculator model. Prices change across OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and other providers, so keep token prices as calculator inputs rather than fixed assumptions in your product plan.

A lightweight AI feature is usually a rewrite, summarize, classify, tag, or short assistant action. The risk is lower because each request has short input, short output, and limited back-and-forth usage.

This is the safest starting point for many indie hackers and SaaS founders. The margin risk usually comes from giving unlimited usage to free users or letting a short feature slowly become a chat workflow.

A ChatGPT API cost for SaaS estimate changes quickly when the AI feature is conversational. Support bots, onboarding assistants, and in-app AI helpers create multiple turns per session, and each turn may include instructions, history, retrieved context, and generated output.

Heavy AI agents, coding assistants, document analysis tools, and multi-step workflows can generate many calls per user. They often send larger context, retrieve more documents, use tools, retry failed steps, and produce longer output.

This is where how much does OpenAI API cost per month becomes a product strategy question. A heavy agent may be profitable for a paid professional tier, but dangerous inside a free or low-price plan without usage caps.

OpenAI API cost per user can look small when you only count input tokens. Output tokens can change the forecast because the model has to generate them, and output pricing is often different from input pricing. Long explanations, code, tables, markdown reports, and multi-step agent summaries can dominate the bill.

The important question is not only monthly API cost. It is whether API cost leaves enough gross margin after payment fees, infrastructure, support, taxes, and product development. Free users and low-price plans need special controls because high AI usage can exceed revenue.

Cheaper models are useful when the task is simple, repetitive, or easy to verify. The mistake is using a cheaper model for work where poor quality creates retries, support tickets, refunds, or user churn.

To build your own OpenAI API monthly cost calculator scenario, start with three versions: conservative, expected, and heavy usage. Keep the same 10,000 registered users, then vary daily active rate, requests per active user, input tokens, output tokens, retry rate, and model route.

A strong production pattern is model routing: use a fast lower-cost model for routine FAQ, classification, and formatting; reserve a stronger model for high-value, ambiguous, or account-risk tickets; escalate billing, legal, and security issues to humans.

Before forecasting chatbot API cost per month, collect a small sample of real support tickets. Include easy tickets, long troubleshooting threads, refund questions, onboarding issues, and cases that should be escalated. Then estimate the token shape of each category.

Support workloads accumulate cost across retrieved help-center text, repeated system policies, growing conversation history, regenerations, tool-call loops, and fallback routes. These levers matter differently from a one-shot token calculator because one customer conversation can invoke the model several times.

Use this workflow when you are deciding whether to ship an AI customer support chatbot, price a SaaS plan that includes AI support, or compare OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini before production traffic arrives.

There are three billing paths to separate before you estimate Claude Code cost: individual subscriptions, Team subscriptions, and usage-based API billing. Mixing them into one number is the fastest way to misread the budget.

For planning, keep subscription price, included usage allowance, extra usage credits, Console/API charges, and the actual invoice as different concepts. A subscription may provide access to Claude Code, but that does not make every API call part of the subscription bill.

A fixed subscription is easier to budget when a person uses Claude Code interactively. Extra usage credits are a separate usage-based path for eligible paid-plan users after included limits are reached. Console/API billing is a third path for automation, scripts, SDK agents, CI jobs, and product workflows where usage should scale with token volume. Team seats are calculated by member, so the first formula is simple.

Annual billing lowers the effective monthly price where Anthropic lists an annual option, but it is not the same as a monthly plan billed at a lower monthly rate. Taxes, regional prices, contract terms, Enterprise agreements, and future plan changes can also change the real invoice.

Calculator results can differ from the final bill because the calculator is a planning model. It does not know your live Anthropic account settings, tax treatment, negotiated pricing, cloud-provider routing, or every future usage policy change.

Claude Team pricing is per member and requires at least two members. As verified in August 2026, Team Standard is $25 per member per month when billed monthly or $20 per member per month when billed annually. Team Premium is $125 per member per month when billed monthly or $100 per member per month when billed annually.

Teams can choose different seat tiers for different members when that matches usage intensity. For example, a small team may keep most developers on Standard and assign Premium only to heavy users. Usage limits are applied per member, while Enterprise pricing should be verified directly with Anthropic.

This is the most important distinction in Claude Code budgeting: Claude paid subscriptions and Anthropic API or Console usage are independent products. A Pro, Max, or Team subscription fee does not automatically offset ordinary API usage.

Paid Claude plans and Claude Console API billing remain separate products. However, eligible Pro, Max, and Team users may be able to purchase or enable extra usage credits after reaching their included plan limits. These usage-based charges are separate from the subscription price and should not be confused with no-cost API credits or general Claude Console API access.

Claude Code may show token cost estimates even when a user works through a subscription. Treat that as a local planning signal, not as proof that the subscription allowance, extra usage credits, or Console/API invoice equals the token estimate.

Cost per developer depends on the billing path. For subscriptions, it is the plan or seat price assigned to that developer. For API billing, it is a usage estimate based on active workdays, sessions, model choice, input tokens, output tokens, caching, and workflow design.

The calculator keeps monthly token usage as the source of usage cost. Coding tasks per developer per active day is a planning assumption used only to divide that monthly usage estimate into a cost per developer work unit. One coding task can include multiple requests, tool calls, retries, or Claude interactions.

OpenAI does not offer an API key with unrestricted free usage. A real API key is tied to an account, usage controls, model access, rate limits, and token-based pricing. Treat websites offering shared, leaked, or resold keys as security and reliability risks, not as a budget plan.

For most real apps, the sustainable path is an official account, a lower-cost model that passes the workload's checks, and strict budget controls. Measure the prompt and output, forecast request volume, and keep a paid fallback plan even when an account qualifies for Free.

A shared, leaked, or resold OpenAI API key is not a cost shortcut. It can be a security and billing problem. You do not control who owns the account, how the key is monitored, what data is logged, whether the key violates terms, or when access will disappear.

The OpenAI API can cost a few dollars per month for a tiny internal tool, tens or hundreds of dollars for an early SaaS feature, or thousands of dollars for a high-volume product. The same API key can be cheap or expensive depending on usage design.

A good developer cost strategy is routing, not guessing. Start with a cheaper model for routine paths, measure success rate, then reserve stronger models for tasks where quality changes the user outcome.

If your real goal is low-cost AI experimentation rather than OpenAI specifically, compare the tradeoffs before you paste private data into a random tool. The right path depends on quality needs, latency, hosting skill, privacy requirements, and whether you want a managed API or self-hosted model.

Unexpected API bills usually come from usage design, not one expensive request. Agents call tools repeatedly. Users paste long documents. Prompts include stale history. Outputs are longer than the UI needs. Retries happen silently. Free-plan users explore more than expected.

Start with one real workflow. Estimate token counts. Choose a model. Add requests per user and active users. Then test a low, expected, and high-usage scenario before deciding whether the feature belongs in a free plan, paid plan, usage-credit plan, or internal-only tool.

AI API cost control is a repeatable operating habit. It combines forecasting, product limits, provider billing controls, prompt optimization, model routing, and regular invoice review. The goal is not to make every AI call as cheap as possible. The goal is to keep AI API spending predictable while preserving the quality users need.

Surprise bills often come from product behavior rather than provider pricing. A model can be reasonably priced and still become expensive if the workflow sends too much context or lets usage grow without limits.

This checklist works for OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, and other AI APIs because the same core drivers appear across providers: token volume, model choice, request frequency, retries, and product limits.

A useful AI API cost control process starts before launch. Pick one real workflow and estimate it from the bottom up: input tokens, output tokens, selected model, requests per user per day, active users, and days per month.

That baseline is not perfect, but it is much better than waiting for a provider invoice. For production planning, add retry rate, cache hit rate, model routing, batch jobs, and cost per successful task.

Provider billing alerts are useful, but product-level limits are usually more actionable. A team should know which customers, workspaces, features, or internal tools are allowed to spend against the AI API budget.

A customer support chatbot can look cheap during testing because each answer costs a fraction of a cent. The bill changes when thousands of users ask repeated questions, paste long messages, or trigger retrieval from a help center.

Document summarization tools can create large input-token costs because users upload long PDFs, contracts, transcripts, or research files. The cost control problem is usually document size, chunking, and output length.

A team AI assistant has a different risk: many people use it lightly every day, but the aggregate monthly volume becomes meaningful. Internal usage can also hide behind one company API key, which makes per-team reporting important.

AI API cost control is not a one-time spreadsheet. It is a workflow: measure tokens, estimate monthly spend, set budget limits, route models carefully, reduce prompt waste, and review real invoices. That habit keeps OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and other API usage useful without turning the next bill into a surprise.

AI API budget limits are guardrails for AI API spending. They can be hard limits, soft alerts, approval thresholds, free-plan quotas, team allocations, feature-level caps, or separate development budgets. The best setup usually combines provider-side controls with product-side planning.

AI apps need monthly API budgets because usage can expand faster than traditional infrastructure cost. Users can paste larger content, agents can run more steps, support volume can rise, and a popular free feature can create real API spend before revenue catches up.

A provider may offer account or project-level billing controls, but the exact behavior and availability can vary. When available, those controls can be useful as a safety net, but they do not explain which feature caused the spend, which customer created the usage, or whether the product can afford the workflow at scale.

A product-level budget is different. It starts from your business model: expected users, requests per user, token size, model route, plan price, margin target, and usage entitlement. It helps you design what should happen before a provider limit is hit.

Start with usage attribution. Attach a customer ID, project ID, team ID, environment, feature, and workflow or agent-run ID to every model call. Record input, output, retries, tool calls, and estimated or billed cost in an application-side ledger so the budget check has an owner.

Use daily limits to contain sudden spikes and monthly budgets to protect the full billing period. A soft alert reports risk without stopping work. A hard limit triggers an application action such as blocking, queueing, switching to a lower-cost route, or requiring approval. Do not assume a provider alert is a hard stop unless the provider's current documentation says so for your account.

The right limit depends on the shape of the workflow. A short classifier, a long document summarizer, and a multi-step AI agent should not share the same budget rule just because they use the same provider account.

This formula is simplified because many providers price input and output tokens separately, and model prices can change. For a better estimate, split input tokens and output tokens, choose the current model route, and add retry rate, cache hit rate, and fallback calls.

These scenarios are not recommendations for exact dollar caps. They show how the first useful budget limit depends on the usage driver. Estimate the workflow first, then decide whether the limit should live at the app, feature, team, user, or environment level.

A monthly AI budget only works if someone checks budget burn before the month is over. Waiting for the invoice tells you what happened, but it does not give you time to change routing, quotas, prompts, or approval rules.

AI API budget limits are strongest when they combine provider spending controls with product-level planning. Set a monthly app budget first, then add team, feature, user, and environment limits where usage can grow. That gives your AI app room to be useful without letting OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or other API costs surprise the business.

AI API cost optimization starts with token usage, not the pricing table. Many SaaS teams overspend because every request repeats long system instructions, RAG context, conversation history, tool rules, JSON schemas, and examples that no longer help the current task.

You can often reduce OpenAI API cost, Claude cost, Gemini cost, and broader LLM cost without changing models by making prompts smaller, more stable, and easier to reuse. The goal is not to starve the model of useful context. The goal is to stop sending the same unnecessary context thousands of times per month.

Most AI API bills are shaped by two variables: how many requests you send and how many tokens each request uses. Model price matters, but the same model can be affordable or expensive depending on whether the app sends 800 input tokens or 18,000 input tokens for the same visible user action.

If many requests share a long stable prefix, make that prefix cache-friendly. Stable content can include product policy, role instructions, style rules, examples, tool definitions, or a standard task rubric that appears unchanged across many calls.

OpenAI's public prompt caching documentation describes caching for eligible repeated prompt prefixes and recommends putting static instructions and examples before variable user-specific content. Treat that as a prompt-structure principle, not a guarantee that every request will be cheaper.

Even when you are not explicitly thinking about prompt caching, prompt order affects repeatability. If reusable policy, examples, and tool rules are mixed with user-specific content, every request becomes unique earlier in the prompt and repeated context becomes harder to reuse or inspect.

Multi-turn AI products need memory of what just happened. A support bot may need the user's last answer. A coding agent may need the decision it made two turns ago. A sales assistant may need the current account constraint. But useful state is not the same as the full transcript forever.

OpenAI's public conversation state documentation describes approaches such as manually passing prior messages, using Responses API state, and chaining turns with previous_response_id. It also notes that previous input tokens in a response chain are still billed as input tokens, so state preservation should be designed intentionally.

A common LLM cost optimization mistake is describing the same tool workflow in natural language on every call: how to validate JSON, which endpoint to call, how to rank candidates, what fields to return, and what to do after each branch. If the workflow is deterministic, it often belongs in code, configuration, or a compact schema instead of a long prompt.

System and developer instructions are easy to overgrow because teams add new rules whenever a model makes a mistake. Over time, the prompt can become long, repetitive, and internally inconsistent. That increases token usage and can reduce stability because the model has to reconcile more instructions on every request.

The best instruction set is not the shortest possible prompt. It is the shortest prompt that reliably protects quality, safety, formatting, and product behavior for the workflow you are actually running.

If every request carries a large policy block, a long tool guide, and several old conversation turns, that repeated context scales linearly with request volume. A block that looks harmless in one test can become the largest input-token driver once thousands of users trigger it every day.

Changing models can reduce cost, but it can also create hidden cost if quality drops and the app needs more retries, longer explanations, manual review, or fallback calls. The more durable question is: what is the cost per successful task at acceptable quality?

AI API cost tracking means monitoring token usage, request volume, active users, model choice, and estimated monthly spend before OpenAI API cost, Claude API spend, or any other LLM API bill grows out of control.

The useful version is not just watching one provider billing total. Track spend by product feature, model, environment, customer segment, team, and workflow so you can explain why the bill changed and what to do next.

AI API cost tracking is the operating habit of recording what your AI workflows send to models, what models return, how often requests happen, which users or teams trigger them, and how those events translate into dollars.

For SaaS founders, developers, product managers, and ops teams, tracking is what connects a monthly provider bill to product behavior. Instead of seeing only a large OpenAI or Claude invoice, you can see which feature, prompt, customer tier, model route, or retry path created the cost.

OpenAI API cost tracking and Claude spend monitoring matter because AI cost grows from small variables that multiply. A prompt can get longer, output can become more detailed, usage can move from tests to active users, and an agent can make several hidden model calls behind one visible action.

Token tracking explains model workload. Dollar tracking explains budget impact. You need both because the same token volume can cost different amounts when model prices, cached-input rules, provider choices, or routing logic change.

Output tokens can matter more than input tokens because many providers price generated tokens differently, and product teams often underestimate response length. A short prompt that asks for a long report, detailed JSON, or multi-step reasoning can produce more billable output than expected.

A monthly invoice is too late for active cost control. Daily views show sudden spikes, weekly views reveal usage trends, and monthly views help finance, product, and engineering teams compare spend against launch assumptions.

A support chatbot should track one row per AI interaction or summarized interaction: customer ID or plan, feature, model, input tokens, output tokens, request status, retry count, and estimated cost. The goal is to see whether support tickets, long histories, or premium fallback models are driving spend.

From there, apply the selected model's input and output prices. Use official provider pricing and invoices as the final source of truth, and treat the calculator result as a planning estimate for budget conversations.

Content generation workflows often have larger output-token risk than teams expect. A title generator may be cheap, but article drafts, product descriptions, SEO briefs, email sequences, and rewrite jobs can produce long outputs across many users.

When one of these signs appears, update the cost estimate immediately instead of waiting for the invoice. Cost spike prevention is mostly about catching the trend while there is still time to adjust prompts, limits, model routing, or rollout speed.

Cost tracking becomes useful when it feeds budget planning. A SaaS team should compare actual request volume, token usage, retry cost, and model mix against the assumptions used for pricing, plan limits, and gross margin.

Cost attribution has two layers. Provider-native reporting gives you coarse groups such as a project, workspace, or API key. Application-side tags give you the finer view that a product needs: customer, feature, workflow, and environment. A provider can report what it billed within its own account structure, but it cannot know which of your end customers or product features caused a model call.

For a practical setup, use a separate provider project, workspace, or key for each product or environment where that provider supports the split. Put a pseudonymous customer_id or tenant ID, feature, workflow, environment, provider, model, input tokens, cached input tokens, and output tokens on every model-call record. Keep the identifier stable enough to sum costs without writing a customer's name into the cost log. Prompt text is unnecessary for cost attribution, so do not log it for this purpose.

To track OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini without visiting three billing dashboards for every product question, write their calls into one log with the same fields. Price those records from one current price table and aggregate by the tags your application supplied. At month end, reconcile each provider's estimated total against its own invoice or cost report, which remains the billing source of truth. Investigate gaps from missing calls, token categories, or price changes before treating a customer allocation as final.

You do not need a perfect internal data warehouse on day one. Start with provider dashboards, billing exports, application logs, and a simple model of token usage by workflow. Then add more detail as usage grows.

AI API cost management means recording usage, assigning spend to the apps, features, workloads, and teams that caused it, and setting budgets with clear alert rules. When costs rise, the owner investigates the workload, takes corrective action, and reviews whether the change helped.

Start with usage records and provider billing evidence. Assign each workload an owner and a budget, then define who receives an alert, what they should check, and which changes they can approve. Review actual spend, the forecast, and open actions each week. The six-step workflow below provides the baseline; the alert table and worked example show how to act on it.

AICostBudget turns workload assumptions and verified model prices into decision support before you change prompts, routes, or budgets. It can estimate a workload, compare model-switch and retry economics, test caching assumptions, and plan a monthly budget. It does not connect to provider accounts or observe production calls automatically.

Give each workload a budget owner and an escalation contact before an alert fires. The rules below are examples based on the percentage of a monthly budget already spent, not industry standards. Adjust them for workload value, billing delays, traffic patterns, and the time needed to respond. A forecast above budget can justify an investigation before any threshold is reached.

An alert is a notification and a decision trigger. A hard spending cap is an enforcement mechanism that limits or blocks paid requests. They are separate controls: a message at 90% does not stop the next call. Check the provider or application settings, their scope, and any propagation or billing delay before relying on a cap.

AICostBudget helps model budgets and possible interventions. It does not monitor live provider spend, send spend-triggered alerts, or automatically block API calls. Your provider settings, application, gateway, or monitoring system must implement the controls you choose.

Illustrative example only, not customer data, a benchmark, or a production result. Assume a 30-day month, a $300 monthly budget, and $120 spent by the end of day 10. The simple linear projection assumes the same daily spending pace continues.

Only 40% of the budget has been spent, but the projection already exceeds it. The owner should investigate now rather than wait for a 50% alert. Actual usage may be seasonal, change with a launch, or stop after a batch job; linear extrapolation is an illustrative estimate, not a reliable prediction of the next bill.

Use one reporting period and a consistent workload grouping each week. Keep actual billing evidence separate from estimates, date every forecast, and name the person responsible for each open action. A compact report can use these fields without becoming a live dashboard.

At the weekly review, compare actual spend with the last forecast, inspect the largest changed workload, and review unresolved actions. An action is not complete just because a setting changed: record whether spend, usage, and task quality moved as expected. Reconcile with provider invoices when available and explain any difference.

AI API cost management is the operating system for AI API spending. It combines cost estimation before launch, budget limits for product planning, cost tracking after launch, and optimization when spend grows faster than value.

Good AI API spend management does not ask only whether OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or another model is cheaper. It asks which feature is using the model, how many requests it creates, how large the prompts are, how many retries happen, and whether the result is worth the cost.

AI API spending becomes hard to manage because the bill is produced by many small variables at once. A single visible user action may include prompt context, retrieval snippets, model output, tool calls, retries, validation calls, and fallback models.

An AI cost dashboard should make cost drivers visible in the same language the product team uses. Provider totals are useful, but the team also needs to know which feature, user cohort, team, or model route created the spend.

The fastest way to find a cost driver is to group API usage by product feature, not only by provider or model. A single model can be cheap for one feature and expensive for another because prompt size, output length, and retry behavior differ.

Weekly review is especially important after a launch, model change, prompt change, new customer cohort, or pricing update. Monthly review is still useful, but it usually explains the bill after the team has already spent the money.

AI API cost management connects provider billing evidence to decisions about workloads, ownership, budgets, waste, routes, and outcomes. Use actual usage and invoices to establish what happened, then use planning tools to test what should change. The useful unit is not only cost per token or call; it is the full cost of an accepted task.

An AI feature can look inexpensive in a prototype and still become painful after launch. One demo request does not show the full monthly cost of system prompts, retrieved context, output tokens, retries, failed tasks, and usage growth.

A practical launch forecast helps founders, product teams, and AI engineers answer a business question before release: if this workflow works and users actually adopt it, can the product afford the AI API spend at 100, 1,000, or 10,000 users?

This guide shows how to forecast AI API spend before launch using a repeatable SaaS budget workflow: estimate tokens, choose model prices, model requests per user, add retry and cache assumptions, compare model routes, and check whether your subscription price protects margin.

The most common mistake is estimating a model instead of estimating a workflow. A workflow includes the prompt, user input, retrieved data, tool instructions, response format, retries, and fallback behavior.

Before launch, use real examples instead of clean demo prompts. Include short, medium, and long user inputs. Include the system prompt, retrieval context, formatting rules, and the answer size your UI can actually display.

For many SaaS teams, the first savings come from reducing prompt waste before calling the API. If a prompt repeats instructions or asks for unnecessary examples, the monthly estimate will be higher than it needs to be.

After you know the token shape, compare model prices. OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, and other providers can have different input prices, output prices, cached input pricing, batch pricing, context windows, and quality tradeoffs.

Do not assume the most expensive model is the only safe option. Also do not assume the cheapest model is always cheaper in production. A weaker model that creates retries, bad answers, or fallback calls may have a higher cost per successful task.

Imagine a SaaS team launching an AI support assistant. They expect 1,000 active users in the first month, with each user sending 8 AI requests per day. A realistic average request includes 1,200 input tokens and 400 output tokens.

Now add production assumptions. If the workflow has a 10% retry rate, the estimate rises to about $295.68. If prompt cleanup lowers average input tokens from 1,200 to 900 and output tokens from 400 to 280, the estimate drops to about $213.31 with the same retry assumption, or about $193.92 before retries.

This example shows why a pre-launch AI API spend forecast is not just a finance exercise. It helps product teams decide output limits, usage limits, prompt structure, model routing, and pricing before users arrive.

Cost per request is helpful, but cost per successful task is more useful for launch planning. If a workflow requires retries or fallback calls to produce a valid answer, the real cost is higher than the first request.

A routed setup can be attractive because it keeps routine calls inexpensive while protecting quality for harder tasks. The goal is not lowest model price. The goal is the lowest sustainable cost at the quality your users expect.

Once you have a forecast, turn it into product decisions. The estimate should influence free-plan limits, paid-plan packaging, fair-use rules, gross margin targets, and which workloads are real-time versus batch.

How accurate can an AI API spend forecast be before launch? It can be accurate enough for product planning if you use real prompt samples, realistic user volume, current model pricing, retry assumptions, and multiple usage scenarios. It will still need to be updated after real invoices arrive.

Should I forecast cost per request or monthly API spend? Use both. Cost per request helps you understand unit economics. Monthly API spend helps you understand whether the feature is sustainable at user scale.

This guide explains how to estimate monthly AI API cost for OpenAI and Claude before usage scales. It is a tutorial for building a forecast from real usage assumptions, not a replacement for the calculator tool.

A SaaS assistant, customer support bot, AI agent, document workflow, or internal automation can send thousands of requests every day. Each request may include a system prompt, user input, retrieved context, output tokens, retries, fallback calls, and sometimes multiple model calls.

When you need to enter real usage numbers, use the site AI API Cost Calculator for tokens, request volume, active users, and model prices. This article explains the workflow behind that monthly forecast.

An API cost estimate calculates how much an application may spend based on monthly requests, input tokens, output tokens, and model pricing. To estimate your AI API cost, define the expected usage for each request and apply the selected OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini model rates.

For a more realistic forecast, add retry rate, cache hit rate, and model routing. A workflow that looks cheap at one request can become expensive when it retries failed calls, sends long context, or routes too many requests to premium models.

Claude is often used for long-form reasoning, document analysis, knowledge-base answers, and product workflows that need strong writing quality. Those use cases can involve larger context and longer outputs, so token budgeting matters.

The important lesson is not that one provider is always cheaper than another. The lesson is that context length, output length, and model selection can change your monthly budget more than the logo on the API endpoint.

For a commercial SaaS product, the best strategy is rarely one model for everything. A better setup is a routing policy: cheap model for simple classification, mid-tier model for normal responses, premium model for difficult reasoning, and a fallback model only when the first call fails.

Cache savings should be modeled only for the portion of input that is actually eligible for cached pricing. A 50% cache hit rate does not automatically cut the whole bill in half because output tokens, non-cached input, and retries still cost money.

A prompt cost optimizer is valuable because it helps teams reduce token waste without changing the core product experience. For many workflows, the first 10% to 30% of savings comes from better prompt structure, not from switching providers.

A customer support chatbot, AI writing tool, document summarizer, coding assistant, or AI agent may send thousands of requests every day. Each request can include system prompts, user input, retrieved context, output tokens, retries, tool calls, and sometimes multiple model calls.

This matters because the cheapest model per request is not always the cheapest model per successful result. A low-cost model that fails often can create more retries, more fallback calls, and a worse user experience.

The cheapest token is the one you never send. Before an AI request reaches OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, or any other provider, teams can often reduce LLM token usage with a few product-side checks.

This step matters because an API cost estimator can only model the tokens you decide to send. A cleaner request lowers input cost, reduces latency, and makes your AI token budget easier to explain to product and finance teams.

A common LLM cost problem is sending the same long instruction block on every request. If that instruction block is 1,500 tokens and you send it 100,000 times per month, you are repeatedly paying for the same content.

Model routing reduces AI model cost by matching each request to the least expensive model that can complete the job reliably. Instead of sending every workflow to a premium model, a product can classify task difficulty first and route simple work to cheaper models.

Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency when your app sends repeated prompt prefixes or repeated context. It is especially useful for support chatbots, AI agents, document Q&A, internal knowledge-base assistants, and coding tools.

Put stable content first and changing content last. Providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini have public documentation around prompt caching or context caching. Always check the current provider documentation and final invoice because pricing rules may change.

Some AI tasks do not need instant responses. Bulk document summaries, dataset labeling, offline reports, prompt evaluation, CRM enrichment, CSV analysis, and monthly internal reports are often better handled asynchronously.

The most important cost-control habit is forecasting before growth. Before launching an AI feature, estimate average input tokens, average output tokens, requests per user per day, active users, model routing ratio, cache hit rate, retry rate, target gross margin, and suggested subscription price.

LLM cost control is not just a technical task. It is product strategy, pricing strategy, and margin protection. If your AI product is moving from prototype to real users, start with the basics: estimate tokens, compare models, optimize prompts, and plan your monthly budget.

Many expensive prompts are not expensive because the task is complex. They are expensive because the prompt carries polite filler, repeated framing, duplicated rules, and background that does not change the model's answer.

This does not mean every answer should be short. It means the prompt should match the product surface. A billing dashboard, support reply, or internal workflow card usually needs focused output, not unlimited prose.

When a provider supports prompt caching or context caching, stable repeated prefixes may be eligible for lower cost or lower latency. Pricing rules differ by provider, so always verify official documentation and invoices.

It is tempting to reduce API cost by switching to a cheaper model first. That can work, but it is risky when the prompt is still noisy. A messy prompt may make a cheaper model fail more often, which increases retries and fallback calls.

Neither side is automatically the largest cost. A document-review request can be input-heavy, while a short prompt that asks for a long report can be output-heavy. Measure the request shape that your product actually sends.

The example below uses a current model from AICostBudget's source-linked pricing data and recalculates whenever that data is updated. The model name, input price, output price, cached-input price when available, and arithmetic come from the data, not from hand-typed numbers.

A short visible user message can still create a large input bill when the application attaches a long system prompt, full conversation history, several retrieved documents, and tool schemas. Inspect the complete API payload, not only the text box the user sees.

A model can't read an .xlsx file as it sits on disk. Before it sees anything, the cells get turned into text, either by your own code or by a provider's file feature. You pay input tokens for that text, not for the file size, so the format the rows end up in decides most of the bill.

To put numbers on it, we built a 1,000-row, 9-column order export (order ID, date, city, product, quantity, unit price, total, status, and a short note on some rows) and counted it with OpenAI's open o200k_base tokenizer. The data is synthetic, and Claude and Gemini use their own tokenizers, so treat the counts as a guide rather than an exact bill.

CSV and TSV come out about the same. A Markdown table adds 14% for the pipes and spaces. JSON is the expensive choice because every row repeats every column name: minified JSON costs 1.76 times as much as CSV, and pretty-printed JSON 2.62 times as much, for exactly the same data.

Output tokens are the response content generated by the model and returned under the provider's billing rules. This can include natural-language answers, summaries, code, classifications, or structured output such as JSON.

Provider treatment of internal or reasoning-related tokens can differ by model and API. Do not assume hidden-token behavior is identical across providers; verify the documentation and billing records for the exact model you use.

Many models list different input and output prices, and some list a higher output rate. That makes generated length an important cost lever, especially for reports, code, long explanations, and agent responses. It does not mean output is universally more expensive or that output always dominates the bill.

Some models in the canonical pricing data expose a cached-input price. Cached input represents eligible repeated request content billed at the provider's listed cached rate instead of the normal input rate. Stable system instructions, repeated document prefixes, or other reusable context may qualify, depending on the provider and model.

The specification for a module, used for loading.

A module's spec is the source for information about the module.  For
data associated with the module, including source, use the spec's
loader.

`name` is the absolute name of the module.  `loader` is the loader
to use when loading the module.  `parent` is the name of the
package the module is in.  The parent is derived from the name.

`is_package` determines if the module is considered a package or
not.  On modules this is reflected by the `__path__` attribute.

`origin` is the specific location used by the loader from which to
load the module, if that information is available.  When filename is
set, origin will match.

`has_location` indicates that a spec's "origin" reflects a location.
When this is True, `__file__` attribute of the module is set.

`cached` is the location of the cached bytecode file, if any.  It
corresponds to the `__cached__` attribute.

`submodule_search_locations` is the sequence of path entries to
search when importing submodules.  If set, is_package should be
True--and False otherwise.

Packages are simply modules that (may) have submodules.  If a spec
has a non-None value in `submodule_search_locations`, the import
system will consider modules loaded from the spec as packages.

Only finders (see importlib.abc.MetaPathFinder and
importlib.abc.PathEntryFinder) should modify ModuleSpec instances.

Base64 content transfer encoding per RFCs 2045-2047.

This module handles the content transfer encoding method defined in RFC 2045
to encode arbitrary 8-bit data using the three 8-bit bytes in four 7-bit
characters encoding known as Base64.

It is used in the MIME standards for email to attach images, audio, and text
using some 8-bit character sets to messages.

This module provides an interface to encode and decode both headers and bodies
with Base64 encoding.

RFC 2045 defines a method for including character set information in an
`encoded-word' in a header.  This method is commonly used for 8-bit real names
in To:, From:, Cc:, etc. fields, as well as Subject: lines.

This module does not do the line wrapping or end-of-line character conversion
necessary for proper internationalized headers; it only does dumb encoding and
decoding.  To deal with the various line wrapping issues, use the email.header
module.

FeedParser - An email feed parser.

The feed parser implements an interface for incrementally parsing an email
message, line by line.  This has advantages for certain applications, such as
those reading email messages off a socket.

FeedParser.feed() is the primary interface for pushing new data into the
parser.  It returns when there's nothing more it can do with the available
data.  When you have no more data to push into the parser, call .close().
This completes the parsing and returns the root message object.

The other advantage of this parser is that it will never raise a parsing
exception.  Instead, when it finds something unexpected, it adds a 'defect' to
the current message.  Defects are just instances that live on the message
object's .defects attribute.

Quoted-printable content transfer encoding per RFCs 2045-2047.

This module handles the content transfer encoding method defined in RFC 2045
to encode US ASCII-like 8-bit data called `quoted-printable'.  It is used to
safely encode text that is in a character set similar to the 7-bit US ASCII
character set, but that includes some 8-bit characters that are normally not
allowed in email bodies or headers.

Quoted-printable is very space-inefficient for encoding binary files; use the
email.base64mime module for that instead.

This module provides an interface to encode and decode both headers and bodies
with quoted-printable encoding.

RFC 2045 defines a method for including character set information in an
`encoded-word' in a header.  This method is commonly used for 8-bit real names
in To:/From:/Cc: etc. fields, as well as Subject: lines.

This module does not do the line wrapping or end-of-line character
conversion necessary for proper internationalized headers; it only
does dumb encoding and decoding.  To deal with the various line
wrapping issues, use the email.header module.

Basic message object.

A message object is defined as something that has a bunch of RFC 2822
headers and a payload.  It may optionally have an envelope header
(a.k.a. Unix-From or From_ header).  If the message is a container (i.e. a
multipart or a message/rfc822), then the payload is a list of Message
objects, otherwise it is a string.

Message objects implement part of the `mapping' interface, which assumes
there is exactly one occurrence of the header per message.  Some headers
do in fact appear multiple times (e.g. Received) and for those headers,
you must use the explicit API to set or get all the headers.  Not all of
the mapping methods are implemented.

Base class for buffered IO objects.

The main difference with RawIOBase is that the read() method
supports omitting the size argument, and does not have a default
implementation that defers to readinto().

In addition, read(), readinto() and write() may raise
BlockingIOError if the underlying raw stream is in non-blocking
mode and not ready; unlike their raw counterparts, they will never
return None.

A typical implementation should not inherit from a RawIOBase
implementation, but wrap one.

The specification for a module, used for loading.

A module's spec is the source for information about the module.  For
data associated with the module, including source, use the spec's
loader.

`name` is the absolute name of the module.  `loader` is the loader
to use when loading the module.  `parent` is the name of the
package the module is in.  The parent is derived from the name.

`is_package` determines if the module is considered a package or
not.  On modules this is reflected by the `__path__` attribute.

`origin` is the specific location used by the loader from which to
load the module, if that information is available.  When filename is
set, origin will match.

`has_location` indicates that a spec's "origin" reflects a location.
When this is True, `__file__` attribute of the module is set.

`cached` is the location of the cached bytecode file, if any.  It
corresponds to the `__cached__` attribute.

`submodule_search_locations` is the sequence of path entries to
search when importing submodules.  If set, is_package should be
True--and False otherwise.

Packages are simply modules that (may) have submodules.  If a spec
has a non-None value in `submodule_search_locations`, the import
system will consider modules loaded from the spec as packages.

Only finders (see importlib.abc.MetaPathFinder and
importlib.abc.PathEntryFinder) should modify ModuleSpec instances.

This module implements specialized container datatypes providing
alternatives to Python's general purpose built-in containers, dict,
list, set, and tuple.

* namedtuple   factory function for creating tuple subclasses with named fields
* deque        list-like container with fast appends and pops on either end
* ChainMap     dict-like class for creating a single view of multiple mappings
* Counter      dict subclass for counting hashable objects
* OrderedDict  dict subclass that remembers the order entries were added
* defaultdict  dict subclass that calls a factory function to supply missing values
* UserDict     wrapper around dictionary objects for easier dict subclassing
* UserList     wrapper around list objects for easier list subclassing
* UserString   wrapper around string objects for easier string subclassing

This module makes available standard errno system symbols.

The value of each symbol is the corresponding integer value,
e.g., on most systems, errno.ENOENT equals the integer 2.

The dictionary errno.errorcode maps numeric codes to symbol names,
e.g., errno.errorcode[2] could be the string 'ENOENT'.

Symbols that are not relevant to the underlying system are not defined.

To map error codes to error messages, use the function os.strerror(),
e.g. os.strerror(2) could return 'No such file or directory'.

The io module provides the Python interfaces to stream handling. The
builtin open function is defined in this module.

At the top of the I/O hierarchy is the abstract base class IOBase. It
defines the basic interface to a stream. Note, however, that there is no
separation between reading and writing to streams; implementations are
allowed to raise an OSError if they do not support a given operation.

Extending IOBase is RawIOBase which deals simply with the reading and
writing of raw bytes to a stream. FileIO subclasses RawIOBase to provide
an interface to OS files.

BufferedIOBase deals with buffering on a raw byte stream (RawIOBase). Its
subclasses, BufferedWriter, BufferedReader, and BufferedRWPair buffer
streams that are readable, writable, and both respectively.
BufferedRandom provides a buffered interface to random access
streams. BytesIO is a simple stream of in-memory bytes.

Another IOBase subclass, TextIOBase, deals with the encoding and decoding
of streams into text. TextIOWrapper, which extends it, is a buffered text
interface to a buffered raw stream (`BufferedIOBase`). Finally, StringIO
is an in-memory stream for text.

Argument names are not part of the specification, and only the arguments
of open() are intended to be used as keyword arguments.

data:

DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE

   An int containing the default buffer size used by the module's buffered
   I/O classes. open() uses the file's blksize (as obtained by os.stat) if
   possible.

Support for regular expressions (RE).

This module provides regular expression matching operations similar to
those found in Perl.  It supports both 8-bit and Unicode strings; both
the pattern and the strings being processed can contain null bytes and
characters outside the US ASCII range.

Regular expressions can contain both special and ordinary characters.
Most ordinary characters, like "A", "a", or "0", are the simplest
regular expressions; they simply match themselves.  You can
concatenate ordinary characters, so last matches the string 'last'.

The special characters are:
    "."      Matches any character except a newline.
    "^"      Matches the start of the string.
    "$"      Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at
             the end of the string.
    "*"      Matches 0 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
             Greedy means that it will match as many repetitions as possible.
    "+"      Matches 1 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
    "?"      Matches 0 or 1 (greedy) of the preceding RE.
    *?,+?,?? Non-greedy versions of the previous three special characters.
    {m,n}    Matches from m to n repetitions of the preceding RE.
    {m,n}?   Non-greedy version of the above.
    "\\"     Either escapes special characters or signals a special sequence.
    []       Indicates a set of characters.
             A "^" as the first character indicates a complementing set.
    "|"      A|B, creates an RE that will match either A or B.
    (...)    Matches the RE inside the parentheses.
             The contents can be retrieved or matched later in the string.
    (?aiLmsux) The letters set the corresponding flags defined below.
    (?:...)  Non-grouping version of regular parentheses.
    (?P<name>...) The substring matched by the group is accessible by name.
    (?P=name)     Matches the text matched earlier by the group named name.
    (?#...)  A comment; ignored.
    (?=...)  Matches if ... matches next, but doesn't consume the string.
    (?!...)  Matches if ... doesn't match next.
    (?<=...) Matches if preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?<!...) Matches if not preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?(id/name)yes|no) Matches yes pattern if the group with id/name matched,
                       the (optional) no pattern otherwise.

This module provides socket operations and some related functions.
On Unix, it supports IP (Internet Protocol) and Unix domain sockets.
On other systems, it only supports IP. Functions specific for a
socket are available as methods of the socket object.

Functions:

socket() -- create a new socket object
socketpair() -- create a pair of new socket objects [*]
fromfd() -- create a socket object from an open file descriptor [*]
send_fds() -- Send file descriptor to the socket.
recv_fds() -- Receive file descriptors from the socket.
fromshare() -- create a socket object from data received from socket.share() [*]
gethostname() -- return the current hostname
gethostbyname() -- map a hostname to its IP number
gethostbyaddr() -- map an IP number or hostname to DNS info
getservbyname() -- map a service name and a protocol name to a port number
getprotobyname() -- map a protocol name (e.g. 'tcp') to a number
ntohs(), ntohl() -- convert 16, 32 bit int from network to host byte order
htons(), htonl() -- convert 16, 32 bit int from host to network byte order
inet_aton() -- convert IP addr string (123.45.67.89) to 32-bit packed format
inet_ntoa() -- convert 32-bit packed format IP to string (123.45.67.89)

The specification for a module, used for loading.

A module's spec is the source for information about the module.  For
data associated with the module, including source, use the spec's
loader.

`name` is the absolute name of the module.  `loader` is the loader
to use when loading the module.  `parent` is the name of the
package the module is in.  The parent is derived from the name.

`is_package` determines if the module is considered a package or
not.  On modules this is reflected by the `__path__` attribute.

`origin` is the specific location used by the loader from which to
load the module, if that information is available.  When filename is
set, origin will match.

`has_location` indicates that a spec's "origin" reflects a location.
When this is True, `__file__` attribute of the module is set.

`cached` is the location of the cached bytecode file, if any.  It
corresponds to the `__cached__` attribute.

`submodule_search_locations` is the sequence of path entries to
search when importing submodules.  If set, is_package should be
True--and False otherwise.

Packages are simply modules that (may) have submodules.  If a spec
has a non-None value in `submodule_search_locations`, the import
system will consider modules loaded from the spec as packages.

Only finders (see importlib.abc.MetaPathFinder and
importlib.abc.PathEntryFinder) should modify ModuleSpec instances.

Serialize ``obj`` as a JSON formatted stream to ``fp`` (a
``.write()``-supporting file-like object).

If ``skipkeys`` is true then ``dict`` keys that are not basic types
(``str``, ``int``, ``float``, ``bool``, ``None``) will be skipped
instead of raising a ``TypeError``.

If ``ensure_ascii`` is false, then the strings written to ``fp`` can
contain non-ASCII characters if they appear in strings contained in
``obj``. Otherwise, all such characters are escaped in JSON strings.

If ``check_circular`` is false, then the circular reference check
for container types will be skipped and a circular reference will
result in an ``RecursionError`` (or worse).

If ``allow_nan`` is false, then it will be a ``ValueError`` to
serialize out of range ``float`` values (``nan``, ``inf``, ``-inf``)
in strict compliance of the JSON specification, instead of using the
JavaScript equivalents (``NaN``, ``Infinity``, ``-Infinity``).

If ``indent`` is a non-negative integer, then JSON array elements and
object members will be pretty-printed with that indent level. An indent
level of 0 will only insert newlines. ``None`` is the most compact
representation.

If specified, ``separators`` should be an ``(item_separator, key_separator)``
tuple.  The default is ``(', ', ': ')`` if *indent* is ``None`` and
``(',', ': ')`` otherwise.  To get the most compact JSON representation,
you should specify ``(',', ':')`` to eliminate whitespace.

``default(obj)`` is a function that should return a serializable version
of obj or raise TypeError. The default simply raises TypeError.

If *sort_keys* is true (default: ``False``), then the output of
dictionaries will be sorted by key.

To use a custom ``JSONEncoder`` subclass (e.g. one that overrides the
``.default()`` method to serialize additional types), specify it with
the ``cls`` kwarg; otherwise ``JSONEncoder`` is used.

Information about how to convert command line strings to Python objects.

Action objects are used by an ArgumentParser to represent the information
needed to parse a single argument from one or more strings from the
command line. The keyword arguments to the Action constructor are also
all attributes of Action instances.

Keyword Arguments:

    - option_strings -- A list of command-line option strings which
        should be associated with this action.

    - dest -- The name of the attribute to hold the created object(s)

    - nargs -- The number of command-line arguments that should be
        consumed. By default, one argument will be consumed and a single
        value will be produced.  Other values include:
            - N (an integer) consumes N arguments (and produces a list)
            - '?' consumes zero or one arguments
            - '*' consumes zero or more arguments (and produces a list)
            - '+' consumes one or more arguments (and produces a list)
        Note that the difference between the default and nargs=1 is that
        with the default, a single value will be produced, while with
        nargs=1, a list containing a single value will be produced.

    - const -- The value to be produced if the option is specified and the
        option uses an action that takes no values.

    - default -- The value to be produced if the option is not specified.

    - type -- A callable that accepts a single string argument, and
        returns the converted value.  The standard Python types str, int,
        float, and complex are useful examples of such callables.  If None,
        str is used.

    - choices -- A container of values that should be allowed. If not None,
        after a command-line argument has been converted to the appropriate
        type, an exception will be raised if it is not a member of this
        collection.

    - required -- True if the action must always be specified at the
        command line. This is only meaningful for optional command-line
        arguments.

    - help -- The help string describing the argument.

    - metavar -- The name to be used for the option's argument with the
        help string. If None, the 'dest' value will be used as the name.

The specification for a module, used for loading.

A module's spec is the source for information about the module.  For
data associated with the module, including source, use the spec's
loader.

`name` is the absolute name of the module.  `loader` is the loader
to use when loading the module.  `parent` is the name of the
package the module is in.  The parent is derived from the name.

`is_package` determines if the module is considered a package or
not.  On modules this is reflected by the `__path__` attribute.

`origin` is the specific location used by the loader from which to
load the module, if that information is available.  When filename is
set, origin will match.

`has_location` indicates that a spec's "origin" reflects a location.
When this is True, `__file__` attribute of the module is set.

`cached` is the location of the cached bytecode file, if any.  It
corresponds to the `__cached__` attribute.

`submodule_search_locations` is the sequence of path entries to
search when importing submodules.  If set, is_package should be
True--and False otherwise.

Packages are simply modules that (may) have submodules.  If a spec
has a non-None value in `submodule_search_locations`, the import
system will consider modules loaded from the spec as packages.

Only finders (see importlib.abc.MetaPathFinder and
importlib.abc.PathEntryFinder) should modify ModuleSpec instances.

OS routines for NT or Posix depending on what system we're on.

This exports:
  - all functions from posix or nt, e.g. unlink, stat, etc.
  - os.path is either posixpath or ntpath
  - os.name is either 'posix' or 'nt'
  - os.curdir is a string representing the current directory (always '.')
  - os.pardir is a string representing the parent directory (always '..')
  - os.sep is the (or a most common) pathname separator ('/' or '\\')
  - os.extsep is the extension separator (always '.')
  - os.altsep is the alternate pathname separator (None or '/')
  - os.pathsep is the component separator used in $PATH etc
  - os.linesep is the line separator in text files ('\r' or '\n' or '\r\n')
  - os.defpath is the default search path for executables
  - os.devnull is the file path of the null device ('/dev/null', etc.)

Programs that import and use 'os' stand a better chance of being
portable between different platforms.  Of course, they must then
only use functions that are defined by all platforms (e.g., unlink
and opendir), and leave all pathname manipulation to os.path
(e.g., split and join).

Support for regular expressions (RE).

This module provides regular expression matching operations similar to
those found in Perl.  It supports both 8-bit and Unicode strings; both
the pattern and the strings being processed can contain null bytes and
characters outside the US ASCII range.

Regular expressions can contain both special and ordinary characters.
Most ordinary characters, like "A", "a", or "0", are the simplest
regular expressions; they simply match themselves.  You can
concatenate ordinary characters, so last matches the string 'last'.

The special characters are:
    "."      Matches any character except a newline.
    "^"      Matches the start of the string.
    "$"      Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at
             the end of the string.
    "*"      Matches 0 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
             Greedy means that it will match as many repetitions as possible.
    "+"      Matches 1 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
    "?"      Matches 0 or 1 (greedy) of the preceding RE.
    *?,+?,?? Non-greedy versions of the previous three special characters.
    {m,n}    Matches from m to n repetitions of the preceding RE.
    {m,n}?   Non-greedy version of the above.
    "\\"     Either escapes special characters or signals a special sequence.
    []       Indicates a set of characters.
             A "^" as the first character indicates a complementing set.
    "|"      A|B, creates an RE that will match either A or B.
    (...)    Matches the RE inside the parentheses.
             The contents can be retrieved or matched later in the string.
    (?aiLmsux) The letters set the corresponding flags defined below.
    (?:...)  Non-grouping version of regular parentheses.
    (?P<name>...) The substring matched by the group is accessible by name.
    (?P=name)     Matches the text matched earlier by the group named name.
    (?#...)  A comment; ignored.
    (?=...)  Matches if ... matches next, but doesn't consume the string.
    (?!...)  Matches if ... doesn't match next.
    (?<=...) Matches if preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?<!...) Matches if not preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?(id/name)yes|no) Matches yes pattern if the group with id/name matched,
                       the (optional) no pattern otherwise.

Filter instances are used to perform arbitrary filtering of LogRecords.

Loggers and Handlers can optionally use Filter instances to filter
records as desired. The base filter class only allows events which are
below a certain point in the logger hierarchy. For example, a filter
initialized with "A.B" will allow events logged by loggers "A.B",
"A.B.C", "A.B.C.D", "A.B.D" etc. but not "A.BB", "B.A.B" etc. If
initialized with the empty string, all events are passed.

Formatter instances are used to convert a LogRecord to text.

Formatters need to know how a LogRecord is constructed. They are
responsible for converting a LogRecord to (usually) a string which can
be interpreted by either a human or an external system. The base Formatter
allows a formatting string to be specified. If none is supplied, the
style-dependent default value, "%(message)s", "{message}", or
"${message}", is used.

The Formatter can be initialized with a format string which makes use of
knowledge of the LogRecord attributes - e.g. the default value mentioned
above makes use of the fact that the user's message and arguments are pre-
formatted into a LogRecord's message attribute. Currently, the useful
attributes in a LogRecord are described by:

%(name)s            Name of the logger (logging channel)

by a unique string. Application areas can be nested (e.g. an area

separated by periods, much like the Java or Python package namespace. So

The io module provides the Python interfaces to stream handling. The
builtin open function is defined in this module.

At the top of the I/O hierarchy is the abstract base class IOBase. It
defines the basic interface to a stream. Note, however, that there is no
separation between reading and writing to streams; implementations are
allowed to raise an OSError if they do not support a given operation.

Extending IOBase is RawIOBase which deals simply with the reading and
writing of raw bytes to a stream. FileIO subclasses RawIOBase to provide
an interface to OS files.

BufferedIOBase deals with buffering on a raw byte stream (RawIOBase). Its
subclasses, BufferedWriter, BufferedReader, and BufferedRWPair buffer
streams that are readable, writable, and both respectively.
BufferedRandom provides a buffered interface to random access
streams. BytesIO is a simple stream of in-memory bytes.

Another IOBase subclass, TextIOBase, deals with the encoding and decoding
of streams into text. TextIOWrapper, which extends it, is a buffered text
interface to a buffered raw stream (`BufferedIOBase`). Finally, StringIO
is an in-memory stream for text.

Argument names are not part of the specification, and only the arguments
of open() are intended to be used as keyword arguments.

data:

DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE

   An int containing the default buffer size used by the module's buffered
   I/O classes. open() uses the file's blksize (as obtained by os.stat) if
   possible.

  - os.sep is the (or a most common) pathname separator ('/' or '\\')

This module provides regular expression matching operations similar to
those found in Perl.  It supports both 8-bit and Unicode strings; both
the pattern and the strings being processed can contain null bytes and
characters outside the US ASCII range.

Regular expressions can contain both special and ordinary characters.
Most ordinary characters, like "A", "a", or "0", are the simplest
regular expressions; they simply match themselves.  You can
concatenate ordinary characters, so last matches the string 'last'.

The special characters are:
    "."      Matches any character except a newline.
    "^"      Matches the start of the string.
    "$"      Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at
             the end of the string.
    "*"      Matches 0 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
             Greedy means that it will match as many repetitions as possible.
    "+"      Matches 1 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
    "?"      Matches 0 or 1 (greedy) of the preceding RE.
    *?,+?,?? Non-greedy versions of the previous three special characters.
    {m,n}    Matches from m to n repetitions of the preceding RE.
    {m,n}?   Non-greedy version of the above.
    "\\"     Either escapes special characters or signals a special sequence.
    []       Indicates a set of characters.
             A "^" as the first character indicates a complementing set.
    "|"      A|B, creates an RE that will match either A or B.
    (...)    Matches the RE inside the parentheses.
             The contents can be retrieved or matched later in the string.
    (?aiLmsux) The letters set the corresponding flags defined below.
    (?:...)  Non-grouping version of regular parentheses.
    (?P<name>...) The substring matched by the group is accessible by name.
    (?P=name)     Matches the text matched earlier by the group named name.
    (?#...)  A comment; ignored.
    (?=...)  Matches if ... matches next, but doesn't consume the string.
    (?!...)  Matches if ... doesn't match next.
    (?<=...) Matches if preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?<!...) Matches if not preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
    (?(id/name)yes|no) Matches yes pattern if the group with id/name matched,
                       the (optional) no pattern otherwise.
